# SAEM

> **Maturity: beta** — see [Feature Maturity](../maturity.qmd) for what this means.

Stochastic Approximation Expectation-Maximization (SAEM) is an alternative estimation method that uses MCMC sampling for random effects instead of MAP optimization. It is more robust to local minima and can handle complex random effect structures, including models with **inter-occasion variability (IOV)**.

## Algorithm Overview

SAEM replaces the deterministic inner loop of FOCE with stochastic sampling, following the Monolix convention with a two-phase step-size schedule.

### References

- Delyon, Lavielle, Moulines (1999). *Convergence of a stochastic approximation version of the EM algorithm.* Annals of Statistics, 94--128.
- Kuhn & Lavielle (2004). *Coupling a stochastic approximation version of EM with an MCMC procedure.* ESAIM: Probability and Statistics 8:115--131.

## Two-Phase Schedule

### Phase 1: Exploration (iterations 1 to K1)

Step size $\gamma_k = 1$. The algorithm explores the parameter space rapidly, with the sufficient statistics being fully replaced each iteration. This allows fast movement toward the basin of the MLE.

By default K1 is **chosen by the run** (see [the automatic stop](#exploration-stop)): at least 150 iterations (`n_exploration_min`), at most 4000 (`n_exploration_max`). Setting `n_exploration = n` instead fixes K1 = n and turns the automatic stop off.

### Phase 2: Convergence (iterations K1+1 to K1+K2) {#phase-2}

Step size $\gamma_k = 1/(k - K_1)^a$, with $a = 1$ by default (`smoothing_exponent`). The algorithm performs a decreasing-weight average, which guarantees almost-sure convergence to the MLE under regularity conditions (the Robbins-Monro conditions need $a \in (1/2, 1]$).

Default: 1000 iterations (NONMEM's `NITER` default).

**Why 1000.** With $a = 1$ the averaging phase removes an offset left by the exploration phase only like $K_2^{-\lambda}$, where λ is the rate at which EM contracts in that direction — a slow, Robbins–Monro regime whenever λ < ½. Traced runs on `warfarin_iov_saem` measured λ ≈ 0.1–0.36 along the ETA_CL / KAPPA_CL ridge, so the estimate largely keeps where exploration ended: at the former 250 iterations an exploration of 500 ended +0.32 (−2 log L, paired over 5 seeds) worse than one of 150 — not because exploring longer hurts, but because averaging could not undo where the longer exploration happened to stop (from poor initial estimates the difference disappears). Lengthening the phase improved every set measured, paired against 250 (automatic exploration): 500 / 1000 / 2000 iterations gave −0.20 / −0.34 / −0.44 on the pk2_big stand-in (10/10 seeds better), −0.23 / −0.30 / −0.36 on `warfarin_iov_saem` (5/5) and −0.08 / −0.11 / −0.19 on `two_cpt_oral_cov`, at +20 / +53 / +120 % CPU. Polyak–Ruppert iterate averaging (exponent 0.7 or 0.8, mean over the last ½ or ¾) was measured as the alternative and is not used: −0.50 on the stand-in but +0.30 (sd 0.67) on `warfarin_iov_saem` and +0.15 on `two_cpt_oral_cov`.

### NONMEM's kernels {#nonmem-kernels}

The E-step samples each subject's η from its conditional distribution by Metropolis–Hastings. With `saem_kernel = nonmem` it runs NONMEM's SAEM kernels (Users Guide 7.5.1, `ISAMPLE_M1/M1B/M2/M3`), per chain per iteration and in NONMEM's order:

| kernel | proposals (default) | proposal |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | `isample_m1` (2) | independent draws from the population density N(0, Ω) — the prior cancels and the acceptance is the data likelihood ratio, so a subject can leave a wrong region in one move |
| M1B | `isample_m1b` (2) | independent draws from the chain's running conditional mean and covariance (its draws since the Ω burn-in, from the 10th on; a covariance that is not positive definite falls back to its diagonal) |
| M2 | `isample_m2` (2) | the block random walk η + s·chol(Ω)·z |
| M3 | `isample_m3` (2) | componentwise sweeps, one η at a time |

The two random walks' scales are adapted towards `iaccept` (NONMEM's `IACCEPT`, 0.4) within NONMEM's `ISCALE` bounds `[1e-6, 1e6]`; how NONMEM itself steps the scale is not documented, so ferx's multiplicative rule does it. NONMEM's `MCETA` is the option `mceta` (default 0, NONMEM's): when larger than `isample_m1`, M1, M2 and M3 each run that many proposals on the first iteration. Measured at NONMEM's `AUTO=2` value of 100 it did not help — `two_cpt_oral_cov` 6 / 20 seeds at its optimum against 10 / 20 without, pk2s and `warfarin_iov_saem` unchanged within noise — so that model's V1–KA trap is not about where the chains start. How well they move is another matter: the [gradient kernels](#gradient-kernels) clear it. NONMEM's mode 1A (off by default there) and its `ISAMPEND` preprocess (a per-subject sample count from shrinkage, under `AUTO=1`) are not implemented.

Measured against the earlier default (`saem_kernel = rw`: `n_mh_steps` block proposals, 6–20, plus the componentwise sweep), both under the automatic exploration stop, 1000 averaging iterations and two chains: the cost per iteration is the same (pk2_big stand-in 4.7 vs 4.55 ms in exploration), but the chain decorrelates faster, so the exploration stop is met sooner — pk2s K1 1260–1560 against 1730–4000, **20.9–23.2 s against 24–42 s CPU** (four seeds, interleaved), with no seed at the maximum (two of ten under `rw`) and median gap +0.04 against +0.18; `warfarin_iov_saem` 1.8 vs 2.7 s at a comparable gap (+0.17 vs +0.10, within IS noise); `two_cpt_oral_cov` 10 / 20 seeds at its optimum against 7 / 20 (8 against 12 in the V1–KA trap), at the same cost.

### Choosing the E-step kernels {#saem-kernels}

Each SAEM iteration moves every chain's random effects with a sequence of kernels, each a Metropolis–Hastings or Hamiltonian move that leaves the subject's conditional posterior unchanged, so any combination is valid. You choose them as counts per chain per iteration; `0` turns one off. They run in this order, broad moves first:

| count | kernel | cost per move | add it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `isample_m1` | independence draw from N(0, Ω) (NONMEM M1) | 1 evaluation | jumps out of a wrong mode |
| `isample_imh` | independence draw from the subject's Laplace approximation, refreshed every `saem_imh_refresh` iterations (f-SAEM, [below](#saem-imh)) | 1 evaluation | near-independent draws on data-rich subjects; outside its scope it runs as `m1` |
| `isample_m1b` | independence draw from the chain's running conditional moments (NONMEM M1B) | 1 evaluation | the same, from the chain's own history |
| `isample_hmc` | Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on the exact η-gradient ([gradient kernels](#gradient-kernels)) | 2–3 gradients | fast, exact local moves along correlated posteriors |
| `isample_nuts` | No-U-Turn transition, otherwise as `hmc` | ~4–30 gradients | an adaptive trajectory length |
| `isample_mala` | Metropolis-adjusted Langevin: one leapfrog step, otherwise as `hmc`, with its own step size | 1 gradient | cheap gradient-guided local moves |
| `isample_m2` | block random walk η + s·chol(Ω)·z (NONMEM M2) | 1 evaluation | NONMEM's local move |
| `isample_m3` | componentwise sweeps, one η at a time (NONMEM M3) | n_η evaluations | coordinates the other moves neglect |

`saem_kernel` is a preset: it fills in every count you did not set, and a count you set overrides it.

| `saem_kernel` | counts |
|---|---|
| `hmc` (default) | `imh 1, hmc 1` (`m1 1, hmc 1` outside f-SAEM's scope) |
| `nonmem` | `m1 2, m1b 2, m2 2, m3 2` — NONMEM's own kernels ([NONMEM's kernels](#nonmem-kernels)) |
| `nuts` | `imh 1, nuts 1` (likewise) |
| `mala` | `imh 1, mala 3` (likewise) |
| `rw`, `imh` | the earlier random-walk and f-SAEM kernels, unchanged; the `isample_*` counts do not apply |

Neither NONMEM nor Monolix runs a gradient kernel inside SAEM: NONMEM's NUTS is a separate full-Bayesian method (`$EST METHOD=NUTS`), and both tools' SAEM E-steps are Metropolis–Hastings kernels set by counts (NONMEM's `ISAMPLE_M1/M1B/M2/M3`, Monolix's m₁…m₄), the convention these counts follow. The default `hmc` targets the same conditional posterior, so SAEM aims at the same estimate. No two implementations reproduce each other's Monte Carlo runs (their random streams differ), so a comparison with NONMEM is of estimates, not iterations; `saem_kernel = nonmem` runs NONMEM's own kernels, the closest algorithmic match.

So `saem_kernel = hmc` with `isample_m3 = 1` adds a componentwise sweep after HMC, `isample_imh = 0` drops its jump, and `isample_hmc = 1` alone adds HMC to NONMEM's four kernels. The fit reports what ran — `saem_kernels: "imh 1, hmc 1"` in `-fit.yaml`, `FitResult::saem_kernels` — and refuses a schedule with every count at 0.

### Gradient kernels {#gradient-kernels}

`hmc`, `nuts` and `mala` move a chain along the exact gradient of its subject's conditional log-density, `−log p(y_i, η_i)` (the same function every other kernel scores with), from the AD engine: the subject's compiled plan, the value from the same pass. Under IOV the move is joint over η and every occasion's κ. A chain the engine gives no gradient for runs two `m2` and two `m3` moves in their place that iteration; if it gives none at all, the fit says so.

Both are preconditioned: the mass matrix is the inverse of the chain's running conditional covariance (its moments from the tenth draw after the Ω burn-in; under IOV the stacked `[η, κ]` moments), so in the integrator's coordinates a near-Gaussian posterior is close to N(0, I). Before a chain has those draws the metric is Ω's own factor. That is deliberate: a metric fitted to the posterior from the start (the Fisher information at η = 0) measured *worse* — the chains settle at once, the exploration stop fires early (two_cpt_oral_cov K1 295 against 455), and that model's V1–KA trap returned on 4 of 20 seeds. HMC integrates for about π/2 in those coordinates (jittered ±20 %), exactly: `n = ⌈T/ε⌉` steps of `T/n`, a nearly independent draw in two or three leapfrog steps (stepping the adapted ε instead overshoots T by up to a step: measured 2.18 against 1.97 steps per transition and ~7 % more CPU on pk2s at the same −2LL); NUTS is Stan's multinomial No-U-Turn sampler to depth 5. The step size is adapted per chain towards an acceptance of 0.8 during exploration and frozen for the averaging phase. MALA is one leapfrog step from a fresh momentum — the Langevin proposal η′ = η − ½ε²·M⁻¹∇U(η) + ε·Lξ under the same metric, accepted with its Metropolis–Hastings ratio — with a step size of its own, adapted towards 0.574 (the optimal MALA acceptance, Roberts & Rosenthal 1998). Consecutive HMC and MALA transitions carry the gradient at the chain's state from one to the next, and the proposal's value comes from its gradient's pass (with IOV too, for a plain Gaussian residual), so a MALA transition costs one AD pass. Unit tests check all three kernels against the exact conditional moments, by quadrature, on a nonlinear model and on the joint IOV posterior, under the exact and a mis-scaled metric.

`FitResult::saem_gradient_kernel` (and `-fit.yaml`) reports the transitions run and declined, the divergences in the averaging phase, the mean leapfrog steps, the averaging phase's mean acceptance and the median step size; a warning names more than 1 % divergences there, a mean acceptance below 0.6, or a step size at its floor.

Measured against `nonmem` (the automatic stop, 1000 averaging iterations, two chains; gap = importance-sampled −2 log L above the reference):

| | `nonmem` | `hmc` |
|---|---|---|
| `two_cpt_oral_cov`, 20 seeds at the optimum | 10 (8 in the V1–KA trap) | **20** (none) |
| pk2_big stand-in, mean gap (5 seeds) | +0.20 (sd 0.19) | **−0.09** (sd 0.11) |
| `warfarin_iov_saem`, mean gap (5 seeds) | +0.19 (sd 0.14) | **+0.02** (sd 0.01) |
| CPU per fit, pk2s | 27.3 s | **23.8 s** |

On `two_cpt_oral_cov` the subjects' posteriors are correlated along the V1–KA direction, which the random walks follow poorly; the drawn ηs then pull Ω and θ toward the trade-off mode. The preset's independence jump (f-SAEM's proposal, or M1 under IOV) ties HMC alone on `two_cpt_oral_cov` and pk2s and is what brings `warfarin_iov_saem` from +0.09 to +0.02. One chain instead of two halves the cost but failed a pk2s seed (+4.6, exploration at its maximum), and a shorter averaging phase loses ~0.02–0.03 per halving on every model while saving little where exploration dominates, so both stay as NONMEM has them. NUTS reaches HMC's quality on `two_cpt_oral_cov` at ~25 % more CPU. MALA (`saem_kernel = mala`, `imh 1, mala 3`) ties HMC: `two_cpt_oral_cov` 20 / 20 seeds at its optimum in 1.9 against 1.8 s, `warfarin_iov_saem` +0.02 in 1.6 against 1.5 s, and the pk2_big stand-in −0.05 against −0.09 (within seed noise) in **21.9 against 26.3 s** (median of five seeds; its exploration stop fires sooner, K1 1640 against 2360). `mala 1` is cheaper still but mixes too little: pk2s +0.37 and `warfarin_iov_saem` +0.21, one seed of five off its optimum on each; `mala 5` costs more for nothing (pk2s 36.6 s). So the preset runs three. An η-only move on the IOV model, κ left to its own random walk, was worse than `nonmem` (+0.50): the joint move matters. Reverse mode over the compiled plan gave the same gradient to 1e-15 but was ~7 % slower at these 2–5 random effects, so the forward jets stay.

### Chains {#chains}

`n_chains` (default **2**, NONMEM's `ISAMPLE=2`) independent η chains are run per subject. Each SAEM iteration draws one η per chain, and the sufficient statistics and the M-step use all of them, which lowers the Monte Carlo noise of every iteration. It is implemented the way Monolix describes its chains — the data set is replicated `n_chains` times for the SAEM iterations (chain 1 keeps the subjects' own random streams), and the final EBEs, OFV and covariance step use the original subjects. (Monolix's own default is to add chains until at least 50 subjects are sampled, `minIndivForChains = 50`.) With the automatic exploration stop and 1000 averaging iterations, two chains against one (measured on the base before main's hashed streams): pk2_big stand-in +1.22 → **+0.73** (mean gap, 10 seeds; sd 0.51 → 0.28), `warfarin_iov_saem` (10 subjects) +0.42 → **+0.11** (sd 0.56 → 0.10). A second chain costs ~1.9× per iteration: the copies are registered with the fit's kernel-JIT scope, so their plan keys are read by address rather than re-hashed per likelihood evaluation (unregistered, they cost 2.5–3×). On `two_cpt_oral_cov` two chains ended a little more often in a ridge region around $\omega^2_{V1}$ ≈ 0.15 (about +2, against the optimum's 0.11; importance-sampled estimation started there walks back to the optimum) — both chain counts reach it and the deeper V1–KA trap on some seeds, so it is a property of that surface, not of the chains: one chain on the data set duplicated is bit-for-bit the two-chain fit. Set `n_chains = 1` for the single-chain SAEM.

### The exploration stop {#exploration-stop}

The convergence phase *freezes* whatever the exploration phase reached: with $a = 1$ the averaging weight of iteration $K_1 + 1$ is 1 and the weights then decay, so a parameter that is still moving at $K_1$ is pinned near where it was. Weakly identified Ω entries are the ones that move slowly: under the exploration cap on the Ω step ($\gamma^\Omega \le 0.1$) a variance component whose optimum is far below its start decays over hundreds of iterations. On the 5-η, 9-θ `pk2_big` benchmark the fixed 150 iterations ended while $\omega^2_Q$ was still at 0.019 (optimum ≈ 0.003), and the importance-sampled −2 log L stayed 10.6 above the optimum (median of 5 seeds); a longer averaging phase barely helps, a longer *exploration* does.

Monolix ends exploration by an automatic stop (on by default) between a minimum of 150 and a maximum of 500 iterations; the minimum is also "the interval length over which the auto-stop criteria are tested", and the criterion watches the stability of the convergence indicator (the complete-data log-likelihood), the Ω parameters and the error-model parameters — the test itself is not published. NONMEM's termination test (Users Guide 7.5.1, §I.46) is opt-in: `CTYPE=0`, the default, runs the whole `NBURN` (default 1000). With `CTYPE` = 1–3 it regresses each monitored quantity (objective, θ, σ; Ω diagonals from `CTYPE=2`, all of Ω at `3`) on the iteration number over the latest `CITER = 10` iterates spaced `CINTERVAL` apart and ends burn-in when no slope is significant at `CALPHA`. The guide stresses the spacing — consecutive SAEM iterates "can be highly correlated", so it advises `CINTERVAL` 10–100, and `CINTERVAL=0` lets NONMEM pick it; `AUTO=1` sets `CTYPE=3 NBURN=4000 CINTERVAL=0 CALPHA=0.05`; and it warns that the test "can often be very conservative", recommending `CALPHA` 0.01 and a large `NBURN`. ferx runs NONMEM's test, `CTYPE=3`, with the interval chosen per coordinate from its autocorrelation.

#### The rule {#exploration-stop-rule}

- **Tracked coordinates.** The complete-data −log L $\sum_i -\log p(y_i, \eta_i;\theta,\Omega,\sigma)$ at the current draws (the `condNLL` that `verbose` prints), θ, log Ω<sub>jj</sub>, the correlations $\Omega_{jk}/\sqrt{\Omega_{jj}\Omega_{kk}}$ (and the same for Ω<sub>IOV</sub>), and log σ. A fixed parameter or structural zero is constant and cannot drift.
- **Test.** For each coordinate, its latest ten iterates spaced `c` apart (NONMEM `CITER=10`, `CINTERVAL=c`) are regressed on the iteration number, and the slope is tested against zero with a Student t (8 degrees of freedom, two-sided 5 %, NONMEM `CALPHA=0.05` as under `AUTO=1`). The spacing `c` is the coordinate's integrated autocorrelation time (Geyer initial-positive sequence, on the linearly detrended series after the 20 burn-in iterations), clamped to 10–50, so the ten points are close to independent. A coordinate whose series is still shorter than `10 × c` is not yet testable and blocks the stop. The test runs every 10 iterations.
- **Why the spacing.** An earlier version of this rule tested five 20-iteration batch means over the trailing 100 iterations. Traced long runs showed integrated autocorrelation times of ~35 iterations at the median and 90–170 at the 90th percentile, so those batches were far from independent: on the stationary tail of the traces each coordinate was flagged 12–23 % of the time against a nominal 5 %, and the rule stopped when, by chance, every coordinate passed in the same window (on the pk2_big stand-in below, ω²<sub>Q</sub> was still 40–90 % above its plateau at the stop). Calibration of the spaced test on simulated AR(1) noise, 2000 iterations: false-trend rate 6.8 % / 6.5 % / 11.3 % at lag-1 correlation 0 / 0.9 / 0.97 (nominal 5 %).
- **Rule.** Exploration ends at the first check ≥ `n_exploration_min` at which every tracked coordinate is testable and none trends, and never later than `n_exploration_max`. The shortest test window is 100 iterations (ten points at spacing 10), the longest 500; an `n_exploration_max` below 100 can never be tested and the fit warns.
- **The Ω exploration step cap is kept.** Removing it alone made the E-step unstable in the investigation that led here; with the automatic stop the cap only slows the decay, and the stop waits for it.
- **Precedence.** `n_exploration` present in the model file (or `saem_n_exploration = Some(n)` in code) is a *fixed* length: `n_exploration_min` / `n_exploration_max` are ignored, no test runs. Absent, the stop is automatic.
- **Reporting.** The length used is `saem_n_exploration` in `-fit.yaml` (`FitResult::saem_n_exploration_used`; `verbose` prints it). If the maximum is reached before every coordinate was shown stationary, a warning says so and names them (still drifting, or too few iterations to test at their autocorrelation; for example `OMEGA(ETA_Q)`) — raise `n_exploration_max` and compare.

#### Measured {#exploration-stop-measured}

A public stand-in for `pk2_big` (2-cpt oral, block Ω on CL/V1, true $\omega^2_Q$ = 0.003 started at 0.08, 300 subjects × 6 samples), the `warfarin_iov_saem` example (10 subjects) and the 5-η `two_cpt_oral_cov` example (30 subjects); `--threads 2`, gap = importance-sampled −2 log L (3000 samples) above the best value reached — for the stand-in, an IMP estimate started from FOCEI (−4802.85, $\omega^2_Q$ 0.0057). Mean gap over seeds:

Measured on ferx with these defaults merged onto main (hashed SAEM streams, `mstep_optimizer = auto`):

| set (seeds) | old default: 150 + 250, 1 chain | **default: automatic + 1000, 2 chains** | K1 (default) | CPU / fit: old → default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pk2s (10) | +4.63 (sd 1.06) | **+0.18** (sd 0.19) | 1300–4000 (2 seeds reach the maximum and warn) | 6.1 → 28.9 s |
| wiov (5) | +0.82 (sd 0.50) | **+0.14** (sd 0.12) | 540–580 | 1.0 → 2.7 s |
| two_cpt_oral_cov (20) | 10 / 20 within 0.5 of the optimum, 9 / 20 in the V1–KA trap (> +5) | 7 / 20 within 0.5, 12 / 20 in the trap | 490–890 | 0.8 → 3.1 s |

`two_cpt_oral_cov` ends in a V1–KA trade-off mode on about half the seeds under either schedule; the difference between the two (3 seeds of 20) is within binomial noise, but leans the way two chains' lower per-iteration noise would suggest (less of the wandering that lets a single chain leave the ridge). On the earlier base, one chain against two at the new schedule measured +1.22 → +0.73 on pk2s and +0.42 → +0.11 on wiov.

Fixed exploration lengths, measured with 250 averaging iterations on the stand-in (15 seeds, median gap): 150 → +5.17, 500 → +2.00, 1500 → +1.97; the 100-iteration batch-means rule this replaces, +3.00.

#### Maximum and smoothing exponent {#exploration-stop-max}

**Maximum.** 4000, NONMEM's `NBURN` under `AUTO=1`. The stand-in stopped at 1300–4000 with two chains (2 of 10 seeds at the maximum, with the warning naming what still drifted); the longest test window is 500, so a maximum near 500 would turn the rule into a fixed length for any coordinate with an autocorrelation time of 50 or more.

**Smoothing exponent.** `smoothing_exponent = 0.7` (Monolix's $\gamma_k = 1/(k-K_1)^{0.7}$) was measured with the earlier 150–500 rule and is *not* the default, because it was worse on an easy model: wiov +0.08 → +0.45 (median gap), pk1 +0.04 → +0.05, pk1_sparse +2.53 → +2.91, against pk2_big +2.94 → +2.54 and corr +0.16 → +0.11. The option is there for users who want it.

**Annealing instead of the Ω step cap.** Monolix keeps the variances large early with *simulated annealing* — each variance may fall by at most 5 % per iteration, $\Omega_{jj,k} \ge 0.95\,\Omega_{jj,k-1}$ — rather than ferx's damped Ω step ($\gamma^\Omega \le 0.1$), which slows every Ω move tenfold. Replacing the cap with that rule (full γ for the Ω statistic in exploration, decrease bounded at 0.95, correlations kept) was measured with the automatic stop and is *not* adopted. On a public pk2_big stand-in (2-cpt oral, block Ω on CL/V1, true $\omega^2_Q$ = 0.003 started at 0.08, 300 subjects × 6 samples; 15 seeds; gap against an IMP estimate, −2 log L −4802.85, MC SE 0.37) the median gap was +3.12 (range 0.99–6.08) against +3.00 (1.23–4.20) with the cap, and +5.17 for the old fixed 150. On the 5-η `two_cpt_oral_cov` example it sent two of five seeds into a worse basin (+18, +16) that the capped runs avoided. (Measured with the earlier 100-iteration rule.)

## Per-Iteration Steps

Each SAEM iteration consists of:

### 1. E-Step: Sampling

For each subject, sample from the conditional distribution of random effects:

$$
p(\eta_i | y_i, \theta, \Omega, \sigma)
$$

Three samplers are available:

#### Metropolis-Hastings (default, `n_leapfrog = 0`)

Two MH kernels run per subject per SAEM iteration (the mixture of Kuhn & Lavielle 2004):

**Kernel 1 — block proposal**: run `n_mh_steps` symmetric random-walk steps $\eta_{\text{prop}} = \eta_{\text{current}} + \delta_i \cdot L \cdot z$, with $z \sim N(0, I)$ and $L = \text{chol}(\Omega)$. This mixes the joint scale efficiently. For **FREM** models the covariate ETAs are near-deterministic (their pseudo-observations pin them to a posterior SD of $\approx\sqrt{\text{EPSCOV}} \ll \sqrt{\Omega_{jj}}$), so a full-scale joint proposal for them is rejected every time and the *joint* acceptance collapses to 0%. Each covariate coordinate is therefore damped in the block move by a factor $\min(1, \sqrt{\text{EPSCOV}}/\sqrt{\Omega_{jj}})$, so the joint step still explores the correlated PK block while the componentwise sweep handles the covariate coordinates themselves. Ordinary (non-FREM) ETAs use a damping factor of exactly 1, i.e. the plain $\text{chol}(\Omega)\,z$ move (issue #895).

**Kernel 2 — componentwise sweep**: for multi-η models, follow the block move with $\max(2, \lfloor \texttt{n\_mh\_steps} / n_\eta \rfloor)$ sweeps that perturb one coordinate at a time, $\eta_j' = \eta_j + \delta_i^{\text{cw}} \cdot \sqrt{\Omega_{jj}} \cdot z$, holding the others fixed. Because the block proposal is shaped by $\text{chol}(\Omega)$, once $\Omega$ drifts toward a high correlation the block move can only travel along that near-degenerate direction; the single-draw Ω M-step then feeds the correlation back into $\Omega$, and during the $\gamma=1$ exploration phase this compounds into a runaway collapse toward a **near rank-1 $\Omega$** (every off-diagonal correlation $\to \pm 1$, one variance $\to 0$). A componentwise move can always shift a single η independently of $\Omega$'s off-diagonals, so the sampled draws are not forced collinear. The kernel is skipped for single-η models (no off-diagonal to decorrelate).

Both kernels are symmetric in $\eta$, so the proposal density cancels and the acceptance log-ratio is the difference of `individual_nll` values, which encodes the prior $N(0, \Omega)$ plus the observation likelihood.

**Acceptance**: $\min(1, \exp(\text{NLL}_{\text{current}} - \text{NLL}_{\text{prop}}))$. Target acceptance rate: 40%.

**Reported acceptance is combined.** The `mh_accept_rate` column in the optimizer trace (and the verbose banner) is the **combined block + componentwise** rate. Reporting the block kernel alone is misleading for FREM-scale $\Omega$: as above, the block move reads 0% acceptance even when the componentwise sweep is mixing the chain perfectly well. If the *combined* post-burn-in rate stays below 1%, the E-step genuinely is not mixing and SAEM appends a warning to `FitResult.warnings` — the sampled ETAs never moved, so the $\Omega/\sigma$ estimates are unreliable (issue #895).

#### Choosing `n_mh_steps`

`n_mh_steps` defaults to `auto`: the block count is sized from the dataset as

$$
\texttt{n\_mh\_steps} = \mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\left[\,2.5 \cdot \frac{n_{\text{obs}}}{n_{\text{subjects}} \cdot n_\eta}\,\right],\; 6,\; 20\right)
$$

i.e. from the observations each random effect has to be informed by. The
resolved count and where it came from are printed under `verbose = true`, and an
explicit `n_mh_steps = <n>` overrides the rule entirely.

Two scope notes. With `n_leapfrog > 0` the count is **not** ignored: HMC replaces
the block kernel for the subjects it can serve, but `n_mh_steps` still governs
the MH-fallback subjects *and* still sizes the componentwise sweep, which runs
after an HMC proposal as well. And `method = bayes` reads the option but not the
rule — under `auto` its η block keeps the historical fixed 20, because the rule
is calibrated on SAEM quantities and, per the kernel split below, what makes a
low count safe on dense data is SAEM's componentwise sweep, which that sampler
does not run. An explicit count applies to both.

The reason it is not a constant is the step-scale controller. On a sparse
population it reaches its 40 % acceptance target at *any* proposal count —
measured at 0.39–0.46 on cefepime, vancomycin, busulfan and pembrolizumab for
every count from 2 to 20 — so each proposal is worth the same fraction of a
move, mixing per iteration is linear in the count, and so is the cost. Twenty
proposals then buy nothing that six do not. The one benchmark where extra
proposals pay for themselves is the one where the controller *cannot* reach its
target: the Emax PKPD model below realises **0.246**, because its conditional
$p(\eta_i \mid y_i)$ is far narrower than the $N(0,\Omega)$ prior the proposal is
scaled by. Observations per subject per η is the cheapest proxy for that
narrowing, which is why the rule reads it.

On that dense model it is specifically **kernel 2** that earns the count, not
kernel 1. Breaking the coupling experimentally (6 block proposals with the 10
componentwise sweeps that 20 implies, against 20 block proposals with the 3
sweeps that 6 implies, 6 seeds each) puts the *sweeps* arm on 20's numbers —
`d_final` 0.043 and cross-seed stability 0.045, against 20's own 0.029 / 0.044 —
and the *block* arm on 6's — 0.102 / 0.138 against 0.091 / 0.132. Raising
`n_mh_steps` is how a model asks for more sweeps today, and at equal quality the
two spellings cost the same wall here (28.4 s vs 29.0 s), so the rule sizes the
block count and lets the sweep count follow ([#1466](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1466)
tracks separating them).

Measured on ferx `e7343462`, 6 seeds, 150 + 250 iterations, IS −2 log L from the
`imp` readout and `d_final` against a 300/700/40 long run of the same build:

| dataset | obs/η | `auto` | IS −2 log L (auto vs 20) | `d_final` (auto vs 20) | SAEM-stage CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cefepime (458 subj, 3 η) | 0.51 | 6 | 4296.3 vs 4294.9 (seed sd 1–2) | 0.078 vs 0.075 | −35 % |
| vancomycin (100 subj, 3 η) | 0.91 | 6 | 1135.3 vs 1135.0 (sd 0.4–0.9) | 0.037 vs 0.033 | −41 % |
| pembrolizumab (303 subj, 4 η) | 1.02 | 6 | 5983.8 vs 5981.2 (sd 4–10) | 0.179 vs 0.115 | −29 % |
| busulfan (600 subj, 3 η) | 2.92 | 7 | 60044 vs 60045 (sd 3) | 0.040 vs 0.041 | −38…−40 % |
| Emax PKPD (100 subj, 2 η) | 8.0 | 20 | unchanged — the rule returns the old default | | 0 % |

CPU is the SAEM stage's user+sys, 3 seeds on an uncontended lane at `--threads 2`.
Busulfan's 7 is quoted as a bracket because the count it resolves to sits between
two measured cells (6 → 4.40 s and 8 → 4.23 s, against 7.10 s at 20) whose costs
differ by less than the run-to-run spread.

#### HMC (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, `n_leapfrog > 0`)

When `n_leapfrog` is set to a positive integer (e.g. `3`), one HMC proposal replaces the `n_mh_steps` MH proposals per subject per iteration. HMC uses the gradient of the individual NLL to make longer, more directed moves through the posterior:

$$
H(\eta, p) = \text{NLL}(\eta) + \tfrac{1}{2} \|p\|^2
$$

with momentum $p \sim N(0, I)$ and a standard velocity Störmer-Verlet (leapfrog) integrator. Acceptance is on $\Delta H$, targeting ~65% acceptance.

**Requirements**: an analytical PK model (no ODE). The HMC gradient is the exact analytic `Dual2` η-gradient (the same one FOCEI uses). A warning is emitted if `n_leapfrog > 0` but the model is out of the analytic provider's scope.

**Per-subject fallback to MH**: `hmc_step` silently falls back to MH for a subject when any of the following conditions hold:
- The model uses an ODE (`[odes]` block present)
- The model has no analytical PK path (no `tv_fn` — pure ODE-only models)
- The Ω matrix has a non-finite log-determinant (degenerate variance)
- The model is outside the analytic gradient's scope (time-varying covariates, oral infusion, SS+reset, or LTBS). A η-dependent expression `obs_scale` is served analytically (since #486), so on a closed-form model it takes the HMC path — only LTBS combined with it falls back to MH.

In a single run with `n_leapfrog > 0`, different subjects can therefore use different samplers. The acceptance rate reported in verbose output and the optimizer trace is an aggregate across all subjects; in mixed HMC/MH runs the target (65% for HMC, 40% for MH) may not be meaningful for the aggregate. The `n_mh_steps` option governs the number of proposals for MH-fallback subjects even when `n_leapfrog > 0`.

#### f-SAEM independent MH (`saem_kernel = imh`) {#saem-imh}

`saem_kernel = imh` replaces kernel 1 — the `n_mh_steps` block random-walk
proposals — with `saem_imh_proposals` (default 2) draws from an **independent**
proposal built for each subject (Karimi, Lavielle & Moulines, *CSDA* 2020):

$$
q_i(\eta) = (1-\alpha)\,N\!\left(\hat\eta_i,\; c\,\Gamma_i\right) + \alpha\,N(0, \Omega),
\qquad \Gamma_i^{-1} = H_i^\top R_i^{-1} H_i + \tfrac12 \tilde C_i^\top \tilde C_i + \Omega^{-1}
$$

centred on the subject's conditional mode $\hat\eta_i$ with the FOCEI curvature
at that mode — assembled by the same code the FOCEI objective takes its
log-determinant from, from the exact η-Jacobian (the closed form's, or the dual
ODE walk's on an ODE model). The mode is tracked
by warm-started Gauss-Newton steps and the proposal rebuilt every
`saem_imh_refresh` (default 5) iterations; once the mode is tracked a rebuild
costs one η-gradient and one η-Jacobian and no NLL evaluation. The search is
seeded from the previous centre, or from the prior mean $\eta = 0$ on the
first build, and never from the chain's current state: Gauss-Newton is capped
at five steps and can stop short of the mode, and a centre that depended on
the current $\eta$ would void the correction below. Because the proposal does
not depend on the chain's current state, the proposal density no longer
cancels, and the acceptance ratio carries it:
$\log\alpha = [\text{NLL}(\eta) - \text{NLL}(\eta')] + [\log q(\eta) - \log q(\eta')]$.
Both NLLs come from the same evaluation the random walk scores, so the two
kernels target the same conditional, and a subject whose curvature cannot be
built takes the random walk until its next scheduled refresh.

The componentwise sweep (kernel 2) still runs after it — it is the
anti-collapse device for a block Ω, and an IMH proposal is not a substitute
(`tests/saem_block_omega_collapse.rs` runs under both kernels). The random
walk's step-scale controller never reads the IMH kernel's acceptance (≈0.8 is
not on the random walk's 0.40 scale).

Three details carry the design:

- **The defensive component** ($\alpha$ = `saem_imh_defensive`, default 0.05).
  On `CL = TVCL·exp(η)` with informative data the conditional can be far flatter
  than its curvature at the mode: on a measured subject the mode sits at
  $\eta_{CL} = 1.5$ with a Laplace SD of 0.074, so $\eta = 0$ is 20 proposal SDs
  out while scoring only 15 objective units above the mode, and a pure Laplace
  proposal accepts **0 of 200** moves from there. Mixing in the prior bounds the
  importance ratio and unsticks it. The main component is also inflated by a
  fixed $c = 1.2$.
- **Two gates, decided before the run.** Scope: an analytical PK or ODE model
  whose η-gradient and η-Jacobian the adjoint's recorder serves exactly (an ODE
  model whose right-hand side and readout the dual ODE walk covers, an SDE
  included; an ODE the walk declines is out), and none of IOV, `iiv_on_ruv`, mixture, FREM,
  `block_sigma`, M3, non-Gaussian endpoint or LTBS. Information: at least
  `saem_imh_min_obs_per_eta` (default 2.0) mean observations per subject per η —
  below that the conditional is barely narrower than the prior, and the
  kernel's premise does not hold. A declined fit runs `rw` with a warning that
  names the reason; the startup banner's `sampler:` line reports the same
  decision.
- **No clock reaches the estimates.** The kernel's cost per subject-iteration
  depends on the model — an η-gradient measured at ~3 NLL evaluations on a
  closed-form 2-cpt model and ~22 on one whose clearance reads `TIME` — and the
  fit reports it as a warning when it exceeds 1.5× the random walk it replaced,
  but never switches kernel on it, so a seeded fit is reproducible.

##### Measured {#saem-imh-measured}

ferx `f8955c24` against the same commit with `saem_kernel = imh`, 6 seeds,
150 + 250 iterations, one thread, one uncontended lane with the arms
interleaved per seed, on macOS arm64. Likelihood is the importance-sampled
−2 log L (`method = [saem, imp]`, `imp_eval_only`, 3000 samples, fixed IS
seed); Δ is paired by seed against `rw`, negative is better; CPU is user+sys of
a SAEM-only run.

| bench | obs/η | CPU vs `rw` | Δ IS −2LL, `imh` | Δ, `imh` + `score_sa` | seed sd, `rw` → `imh` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| warfarin (10 subj, 3 η) | 3.67 | −40 % (0.033 → 0.020 s) | −0.000 ± 0.002 | −0.001 ± 0.001 | 0.001 → 0.002 |
| busulfan, first 100 | 2.31 | −2 % | **−2.20 ± 1.18 (6/6)** | **−3.39 ± 1.26 (6/6)** | 1.26 → 0.37 |
| busulfan 600, TVQ fixed | 2.92 | −9 % | −0.38 ± 1.03 | +0.51 ± 1.24 | 1.28 → 0.57 |
| busulfan 600, TVQ free | 2.92 | −3 % | **+5.16 ± 5.44 (1/6)** | −1.97 ± 5.37 | 2.29 → 3.98 |

What this says:

- **It is a quality lever, not a speed lever.** The speed programme measured
  −40…−50 % CPU against a random walk of 20 proposals; since `n_mh_steps = auto`
  (#1468) the random walk spends 6–9, and on busulfan the two kernels cost the
  same to within the run-to-run spread. (Warfarin's −40 % is two 10 ms timer
  ticks.)
- **Where it pays** is a data-rich model whose random effects carry all the
  structure: on the 100-subject busulfan subset it is better on every seed and
  3.4× tighter across seeds, and lands where NONMEM 7.5.1's SAEM does — ferx's
  importance-sampled −2 log L at NONMEM's own SAEM estimates (three seeds) is
  7531.0, 7531.8 and 7532.1, against 7533.8 ± 1.3 for `rw` and 7531.6 ± 0.4 for
  `imh`.
- **Pair it with `mstep_solver = score_sa` when a θ has no η.** With busulfan's
  `TVQ` free, `imh` alone is worse: TVQ, which the M-step estimates from one
  draw per iteration, spreads 9.2–12.0 across seeds against 9.2–10.2 under

  iteration. `score_sa` averages the score rather than the maximiser, and the
  pairing is tie-or-better on all four benches. It costs CPU on busulfan

  `imh` with such a θ under `bobyqa` says so in its warnings.
- **Where it does not run.** The information gate declines the sparse benches —
  cefepime 0.51 obs/η, pembrolizumab 1.02. ODE models were out of scope when
  this table was measured; they are in scope since #2639, measured below.

The E-step sampling is parallelized across subjects using Rayon.

The startup banner reports the resolved E-step kernel on a `sampler:` line, e.g. `sampler:  Metropolis-Hastings random walk` or `sampler:  HMC (3 leapfrog steps, Dual2 analytic gradients)`. If `n_leapfrog > 0` but HMC is unavailable (an ODE model, or one outside the analytic gradient's scope), the line says so and reflects the MH fallback. Because SAEM is sampling-based rather than gradient-driven, it does not print the `gradient:` line that FOCE/FOCEI use — the `gradient_method` option only governs the inner EBE/Hessian step (used for diagnostics, and consumed by a following `imp` stage), not the SAEM iterations themselves.

### 2. Stochastic Approximation Update

Update the sufficient statistic for $\Omega$:

$$
S_2 \leftarrow (1 - \gamma_k^\Omega) \cdot S_2 + \gamma_k^\Omega \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \eta_i \eta_i^T
$$

**Damped Ω step.** The θ M-step uses the full $\gamma_k$ (1.0 during exploration), but the Ω sufficient statistic uses a *capped* step $\gamma_k^\Omega = \min(\gamma_k, 0.1)$. With the full $\gamma=1$, Ω would be overwritten every exploration iteration by a single warm-started, not-yet-equilibrated MCMC draw; for a correlated block that one snapshot is biased toward the chain's current correlation, and the bias feeds back through $\mathrm{chol}(\Omega)$ into the next proposal — the same rank-1 runaway the componentwise kernel guards against, here attacked from the M-step side. Capping the Ω learning rate during exploration averages those draws (Robbins-Monro) and breaks the feedback while θ still moves at full speed. The cap applies during exploration only; in the convergence phase it is lifted and Ω uses the full decaying $\gamma_k = 1/(k-K_1)$ — the same Robbins-Monro schedule as θ — so the SA estimate settles correctly (by then the chain is equilibrated, so the single-draw overwrite risk no longer applies).

**Damped σ step.** The residual σ that rides the numerical M-step gets its own capped step, $\gamma_k^\sigma = \min(\gamma_k,\,0.2,\,\gamma_k^\theta)$, applied to $\sigma^2$ rather than to $\log\sigma$ (issue #1445). Until then it was the one SAEM statistic with no stochastic approximation at all — assigned outright in both phases — so the reported σ was a single draw of the M-step maximiser rather than its average. The cap is on in **both** phases, which is what distinguishes it from the Ω step: Ω accepts the $\gamma=1$ assignment at the first convergence iteration because $(1/N)\sum_i \eta_i\eta_i^T$ over $N$ subjects is a well-determined statistic, while the σ maximiser of a *minority* variance component is not. The additive half of a `combined(PROP, ADD)` model on sparse data is exactly that: its single-draw conditional maximiser is boundary-heavy, so an assigned σ reports whichever value the last iteration happened to draw. Beyond $k-K_1 = 5$ the cap no longer binds and the full decaying $\gamma_k = 1/(k-K_1)$ takes over, which is what lets the SA estimate settle. Averaging on the variance scale is deliberate — it is the scale the [scalar residual sufficient statistic](#scalar-residual-error-update) already averages on, and a geometric mean of a sequence with mass near zero collapses where the arithmetic mean of $\sigma^2$ does not (measured: $\log\sigma$ averaging leaves the #1445 fixture's $\sigma_{\text{add}}$ at 0.47 against a truth of 1.8, where the $\sigma^2$ average reaches 1.4). The third term is one-sided: σ never steps *faster* than θ, but the two are not always equal. They are equal during **exploration** whenever `mstep_damping` is at or below 0.2 (the `iiv_on_ruv` default of 0.03 is), and from the fifth convergence iteration on, where $1/(k-K_1) \le 0.2$. They differ over the four hand-off iterations $k-K_1 \in \{1,2,3,4\}$ — θ takes 1, ½, ⅓, ¼ while σ takes 0.2 — and during exploration for any `mstep_damping` above 0.2, where σ is the slower of the two. So no configuration, `iiv_on_ruv` included, is bit-identical to before; what is preserved is that σ is never given a larger step than the θ it shares a maximiser with.

#### Which σ components the exploration cap applies to {#saem-sigma-cap-release}

Since issue #1464 the exploration half of that cap is **per component**. The cap protects a variance component that the data identify only weakly. For one the data pin down, it only slows σ's exploration trajectory. That trajectory reaches every θ without an ETA through the same frozen-η objective the numerical M-step maximises. At each exploration M-step ferx computes the standard error of $\log\sigma_k$ under that objective, from the inverse of the σ–σ block of its expected information at the current draw:

$$
I_{ab} = \tfrac12 \sum_j \frac{\partial V_j/\partial\log\sigma_a \;\, \partial V_j/\partial\log\sigma_b}{V_j^2}.
$$

The block is inverted rather than read off its diagonal, so two components the data cannot tell apart both read as weak. A component with $\mathrm{SE}(\log\sigma_k) \le 0.10$ takes θ's step, $\min(\gamma_k, \gamma_k^\theta)$, and keeps the guarantee that σ never steps faster than θ. Every other component keeps the 0.2 cap. The convergence hand-off is unchanged for every component.

That standard error is how far one draw's maximiser of the component can wander, in log units. Measured along 6-seed fits, cefepime's additive term reads 0.15–0.24 throughout exploration. Busulfan's additive term starts at 0.64 from its 1.0 initial estimate (a minority at that point, so it is correctly held) and falls to 0.06 once it has grown to its converged ~28. Every proportional term reads 0.01–0.03. On importance-sampled −2 log L over the same 6 seeds, against the cap on every component:

| | cefepime (run64) | busulfan, 600 subjects | busulfan, `TVQ` FIX |
|---|---|---|---|
| release at SE ≤ 0.10 (shipped) | −0.2 | **−15.6** | −5.9 |
| release every component | +1.0 | −14.3 | −4.7 |

The table hides the readout that fails. Releasing every component puts cefepime's `ADD_ERR` at 0.051 and 0.104 on two seeds in six, which is #1445 again. The shipped gate keeps all six at 1.22–1.41, up from 1.10–1.25 with the cap everywhere and closer to NONMEM FOCEI's 1.550 on the same data. On busulfan the no-ETA `TVQ` moves from 11.7–15.3 to 8.8–11.5; the `TVQ`-FIX control sits at 8.44.

The release applies only in the plain Gaussian scope of [`mstep_solver = score_sa`](#saem-mstep-jensen), and not to `iiv_on_ruv` models. An `iiv_on_ruv` σ shares a ridge with ω_RUV, and the conditional standard error misreads that ridge. Outside that scope the schedule is the #1445 one unchanged.

### 3. M-Step for Omega (Closed Form)

$$
\Omega_k = S_2
$$

with structurally-zero entries (cross-block off-diagonals, standalone-vs-block off-diagonals, and all off-diagonals in a fully-diagonal Ω) zeroed out — the SA accumulator $(1/N) \sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^T$ is dense by construction, but the model declares which entries are free parameters. Without this projection the chain feeds spurious sampling correlations into the next iteration's MH proposal Cholesky and Ω drifts toward rank-deficiency. Free diagonals are then floored at `1e-6` to keep them away from zero (which would collapse the per-eta proposal scale `δ·chol(Ω)`); this floor does not by itself guarantee positive-definiteness of a full block Ω.

**Burn-in.** This M-step is suppressed for the first `omega_burnin` iterations (default 20, clamped to the exploration length — `n_exploration_min` under the automatic stop): Ω is held at its starting value while the MH chain warms up. The MH proposal scale is $\delta_i \cdot \mathrm{chol}(\Omega)$, so Ω and the sampler are coupled. On sparse data (few observations per subject) a cold-start chain (η = 0, only `n_mh_steps` proposals) produces a tiny $(1/N) \sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^T$; with $\gamma_1 = 1$ the M-step would install that as Ω on iteration 1, shrinking the proposal, which keeps the chain near zero — a self-reinforcing collapse that dumps between-subject variability into the residual error. The SA statistic $S_2$ is still refreshed each burn-in iteration (at the damped rate $\gamma_k^\Omega$, so it is a running average of the warming chain), so the first Ω update after burn-in reflects the warmed-up chain rather than the cold-start spread. Set `omega_burnin = 0` to disable the burn-in; note that the damped Ω step above now also guards this cold-start collapse on its own (it is a strict generalisation — continuous rather than for the first `omega_burnin` iterations only), so disabling the burn-in no longer reproduces the collapse by itself.

### 4. M-Step for Theta and Sigma (Optimization) {#4-m-step-for-theta-and-sigma-optimization}

Minimize the conditional observation negative log-likelihood with ETAs held fixed:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} \left[ \frac{1}{2} \log V_{ij} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{(y_{ij} - f_{ij})^2}{V_{ij}} \right]
$$

#### Closed-form EM update for mu-referenced thetas {#saem-mstep-closed-form}

When `mu_referencing = true` (the default), ferx detects mu-referenced parameters from the `[individual_parameters]` block and applies the **closed-form EM update** for those thetas instead of running NLopt:

$$
g(\theta_j) \leftarrow g(\theta_j) + \gamma_k \cdot \overline{\eta_j}
$$

where $\overline{\eta_j} = (1/N) \sum_i \eta_{i,j}$ is the empirical mean of the post-MH random effects for the eta paired with $\theta_j$, and $g$ is the mu-scale link. For a mu-referenced model where $P_i = g^{-1}(g(\theta) + \eta_i)$ with $\eta_i \sim N(0, \omega^2)$, this is exactly the M-step that maximises the complete-data log-likelihood, scaled by the SA step size $\gamma_k$ — and it is *link-independent*: the same shift is the maximiser for $g = \log$, $g = \mathrm{id}$ and $g = \mathrm{logit}$ alike. After the update the etas are re-centred by the same shift so they remain deviations from the new $g(\theta_j)$.

What decides eligibility is therefore not the link but whether the **packed** theta — the quantity the optimiser actually steps — *is* $g(\theta)$. ferx packs a theta as $\log \theta$ when its lower bound is non-negative and as $\theta$ otherwise, so:

| Form | mu scale $g(\theta)$ | Closed-form EM update |
|------|----------------------|------------------------|
| `P = THETA * exp(ETA)`, `exp(log(THETA) + ETA)` | $\log \theta$ | yes (theta is log-packed) |
| `P = inv_logit(THETA + ETA)` | $\theta$ | yes — a logit-scale theta has a negative lower bound, so it is packed as-is (#918) |
| `P = inv_logit(logit(THETA) + ETA)` | $\mathrm{logit}\,\theta$ | no — no packing has that scale |
| `P = THETA + ETA` | $\theta$ | yes, on the natural scale whatever the packing — see [additive mu-references](#saem-mstep-additive) (#2540) |

The excluded form is still mu-referenced (it still centres the inner/E-step search); it just takes the numeric M-step. This matters most for bounded $(0,1)$ parameters — bioavailability, pathway fractions, $E_{max}$ fractions — in models that also carry IIV on the residual error, where the numeric M-step works from noticeably noisier conditional samples: declare the theta on the logit scale (`theta LOGIT_F(-0.477, -10.0, 10.0)`) and write `F = inv_logit(LOGIT_F + ETA_F)`.

The packing rule cuts both ways, and a mismatch is reported rather than silently routed: a lognormal theta declared with a *negative* lower bound is packed on the identity scale, and a logit-scale theta declared with a *non-negative* lower bound (`theta LOGIT_F(0.5, 0.0, 5.0)`) is packed on the log scale. Neither packed value is the mu, so the closed form does not apply; SAEM and IMP/IMPMAP estimate such a theta through the numerical M-step and emit an advisory naming it, with the bound to change. Under `mu_referencing = false` **SAEM** runs no closed-form shift at all and suppresses the advisory; single-population IMP/IMPMAP is different — its shift is EM-mandatory, so it runs (and advises) independently of that option, as [the IMP/IMPMAP page](impmap.qmd) describes.

A theta that anchors **more than one** eta (`F1 = inv_logit(LOGIT_F + ETA_F1)` *and* `F2 = inv_logit(LOGIT_F + ETA_F2)`, or the lognormal `CL = TVP*exp(ETA_CL)` / `V = TVP*exp(ETA_V)`) is also routed to the numerical M-step with an advisory: the closed form shifts a packed theta by one eta mean and pins it, and no single such shift is the joint maximiser. Give each eta its own typical value to get the closed-form update.

#### Additive mu-references {#saem-mstep-additive}

An additive typical value, `E0 = TVE0 + ETA_E0`, has $g = \mathrm{id}$, so its mu is
the natural $\theta$. A theta with a non-negative lower bound is packed as
$\log\theta$, so the packed value is not the mu. Since
[#2540](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2540) SAEM shifts the natural
value instead, $\theta \leftarrow \theta + \gamma_k\,\overline{\eta}$, clamps it to the
bounds, repacks it, and re-centres the etas by the change it actually made. The same
update applies to an identity-packed theta. This is single-population SAEM only. Under
a `[mixture]` an additive anchor stays on the numerical M-step, since the class-aware
shift has no additive arm, and SAEM names it in a warning
(`the additive mu-referenced typical value(s) … are estimated by the numerical M-step in
this [mixture] model`,
[#2548](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2548)). Check such a value against
a FOCEI fit, or write the parameter log-normal with a non-negative lower bound, which the
class-aware shift covers. A log-normal theta with a negative lower bound is identity-packed
and stays on the numerical M-step as well. IMP and IMPMAP step the packed value, so for
them an additive theta takes the numerical M-step too, which is why FOCEI is the check.

The typical value can have a line of its own or share one with other terms. Since
[#2544](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2544) these two are the same
mu-reference:

```
E0   = TVE0 + ETA_E0
BASE = E0 + PLACEBO + KAPPA_ARM

BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_E0 + KAPPA_ARM
```

A line is recognised when it adds one bare theta, one eta, and terms that read
neither; the terms may read kappas, covariates and other thetas. NONMEM writes the
same thing as `MU_1 = THETA(1)` with `E0 = MU_1 + ETA(1)` or
`BASE = MU_1 + PLA + ETA(1)`; the two streams end bit-identical
(`nonmem_anchor/saem_additive_mu_inline.ctl`). The theta and the eta must enter the
model only through that line, in either spelling. When another block reads the theta,
or another individual parameter that the model reads does, or another line reads the
eta, the anchor is dropped and SAEM warns `not mu-referenced: BASE`: the shift sets the
theta to the mean of $\theta + \eta_i$, which is the M-step only if nothing else
moves with it. [Individual parameters](../model-file/individual-parameters.qmd#sec-typical-own-line)
lists the shapes that are not recognised.

Without the shift, an additive theta sits on a ridge. With the etas frozen, the data
determine only $\theta + \overline{\eta}$. The split between the two is set only by
the eta prior, which reaches $\theta$ only through later E-steps, and the offset in
$\overline{\eta}$ is added to $\omega^2$. On `tests/data/mbma_placebo`, where the
FOCEI objective is the exact likelihood (minimum 97.0700), SAEM stopped 1–11 OFV
units above the minimum on five seeds, with TVE0 4.7 low and $\omega^2$ 30.3 against
4.81. NONMEM SAEM without `MU_` does the same. With only TVE0 and $\omega^2$ free
(`nonmem_anchor/saem_additive_mu.ferx`), measured on five seeds:

| | OFV (MLE 165.8260) |
|---|---|
| ferx, `BASE = TVE0 + PLAFIX + ETA_E0` before #2544, or with TVE0 read elsewhere | 168.54 – 172.76 |
| NONMEM, no `MU_` | 167.41 – 174.32 |
| ferx, `E0 = TVE0 + ETA_E0`, and `BASE = TVE0 + PLAFIX + ETA_E0` since #2544 | 165.8260 – 165.8266 |
| NONMEM, `MU_1` | 165.8260 – 165.8261 |

On the full `mbma_placebo` model with the split spelling, SAEM lands at 97.33–98.39.
The rest of the gap comes from the 21 thetas still on the numerical M-step
([#2470](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2470)). For a model that is
linear in its etas, as this one is, FOCEI is the exact likelihood and the better
estimator to report.

NLopt still runs for any remaining thetas (non-mu-referenced); the closed-form-updated thetas are pinned at their new values for the NLopt call.

#### Covariate mu-references: typical values that read several thetas {#saem-mstep-covariate-mu-ref}

A typical value that reads **two or more** thetas has no single anchor:

```
CL = (TVCL + (CRCL - 90) * TH_CRCL) * exp(ETA_CL)   # additive covariate
CL = TVCL * (WT / 70) ^ TH_WT * exp(ETA_CL)           # estimated exponent
F  = inv_logit(LOGIT_F + TH_SEX * SEX + ETA_F)        # logit-scale covariate
```

Before [#619](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/619) every theta in such a value sat on the numerical M-step, which holds each subject's sampled η fixed. That is the wrong coordinate system for a covariate slope: once the MH sampler has let η absorb the covariate-correlated part of the between-subject variation, the slope sees almost no gradient, and the two drift together — on the fluconazole model of #619 the renal gradient reached its bound at 0.

ferx now records such a value as a **covariate mu-reference** (all its thetas, one eta) and gives it the mu-referencing M-step in its general form. Holding each subject's $\phi_i = g(A_i(\theta)) + \eta_i$ fixed, the group's thetas are re-fitted to the population of individual values:

$$
\hat\theta = \arg\min_\theta \; \sum_i \tfrac12\,(\phi_i - g(A_i(\theta)))^\top \Omega^{-1} (\phi_i - g(A_i(\theta))) \;+\; \sum_i -\log p(y_i \mid \phi_i, \theta)
$$

with $A_i$ the eta-free typical value at subject $i$'s covariates and $g$ the link (`log` or the logit-scale identity). The data term drops out — and the step is an exact nonlinear least-squares fit (Gauss–Newton) — when three things hold: every covariate the value reads is **constant within each subject**, no estimated theta of the group is read **anywhere else in the model**, and no *other* individual parameter reads the group's **eta**. Otherwise the term stays live and the sum is minimised numerically (BOBYQA), still in the $\phi$-frozen coordinates. A covariate that **varies within a subject** leaves a $\theta$-dependence through the within-subject ratio $A_i(t)/A_i(t_0)$; a theta the model reuses — `CL = (TVCL + TH_X*WT) * exp(ETA_CL)` alongside `V = TVV + TH_X` — leaves one through that other parameter, since preserving $\phi_{CL}$ pins `CL` but not `V`; an eta the model reuses — the same `CL` alongside `V = TVV * exp(0.5*ETA_CL)` — leaves one through the re-centring, which holds $\phi_{CL}$ fixed but moves `V`. ferx detects both kinds of reuse and says so in a fit warning naming the theta or the eta. The new estimate is blended with the same SA step $\gamma_k$ as the single-anchor shift, and each η is re-centred by the change in its own mu so $\phi_i$ is unchanged. This is NONMEM's `MU_1 = LOG(THETA(1) + (CRCL-90)*THETA(2))` — a MU that is nonlinear in THETA — done automatically.

##### Typical values that share a theta

Covariate mu-references that **share an estimated theta** are one group ([#1620](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1620)). In `examples/two_cpt_oral_cov.ferx`, `CL` and `V1` both read `THETA_WT`. Stepping them one at a time cannot work: a step over CL's thetas alone holds $\eta_{V1}$ as drawn — the η-frozen coordinates #619 removed for a single typical value — so $\phi_{V1}$ absorbs V1's half of every move of `THETA_WT`, and the exponent drifts to its bound (SAEM put it at 0.0101 against NONMEM's 0.662). The joint step fits the union of the thetas to every member's $\phi_i$ under the full $\Omega^{-1}$ form and re-centres every member's eta. A theta read only by the members is not "read elsewhere", so such a group still takes the exact engine; one also read outside every group, or by a mu-reference that was itself declined, keeps the data term. A fit warning names the etas and the shared theta. A shared `FIX`ed theta links nothing.

##### A theta that anchors another eta

A covariate mu-reference can also read the theta that **anchors another eta** on its own ([#1630](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1630)) — `V1 = TVV2 * TH_R * (WT/70)^THETA_WT_V1 * exp(ETA_V1)` next to `V2 = TVV2 * exp(ETA_V2)`. Two channels moving `TVV2` in one iteration would have no joint optimum, and declining the group (as ferx did before #1630) left its covariate exponent on the η-frozen numerical M-step, where it wandered (`THETA_WT_V1` 0.68 / 1.07 / 0.63 over three seeds against FOCEI's 0.577). Instead the anchor joins the group as a one-theta member: its closed-form shift is dropped, and the joint step fits `TVV2` to both etas' $\phi_i$ and re-centres both. When nothing else reads `TVV2`, the exact engine still runs. If that other eta has a covariate mu-reference of its own, its anchor never runs, so there is nothing to collide with: the two groups simply share the theta and merge as above. A group is still declined when the anchor's eta has an IIV below `1e-3`, or when the anchor's typical value is not on a log or logit scale (`TVV2 + ETA_V2`), and the warning says which.

##### Scope, and when a group is declined

A covariate mu-reference is used by SAEM and IMP/IMPMAP only; `mu_refs` (inner-loop centring, `suggest_start`, reporting) is unchanged, so FOCE/FOCEI/Laplace fits are byte-identical with and without one. It is declined — with a warning naming the thetas, which are then estimated as if it were absent — when the eta's initial IIV is below `1e-3`, when every theta of the group is `FIX`ed, under a mixture model, and under `mu_referencing = false`. A group step also stands down for one iteration when the typical value is not finite for some subject at the current θ — an additive form such as `TVCL + (CRCL-90)*TH_CRCL` can go ≤ 0 for a low-covariate subject — and the fit reports how many iterations that happened on, since the thetas were then moved by the numerical M-step (or, under IMP/IMPMAP, left to it) rather than by the group. A value that reads `TIME`, `MIXNUM`, a second eta, or a local variable that an `if` assigns in only some of its arms (or from a theta) is not recorded at all; a covariate local every arm of an `if` / `else` assigns, and a `min` / `max` of one, are seen through ([#1422](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1422)).

#### Scalar residual-error update

For a single, free additive or proportional residual SD in a single-population,
uncensored Gaussian model whose free structural thetas are all log-mu-referenced,
SAEM also averages the residual sufficient statistic instead of replacing the SD
with the latest MCMC draw's conditional optimum. For additive error it stores

$$
S_r \leftarrow (1-\gamma_k)S_r + \gamma_k\sum_{ij}(y_{ij}-f_{ij})^2,
\qquad \sigma = \sqrt{S_r/n_{\mathrm{obs}}}.
$$

For proportional error, the summand is divided by $f_{ij}^2$. This reduces
otherwise persistent final-draw Monte Carlo noise in the residual SD. It is an
internal exact M-step for that restricted likelihood, not a new fit option.
Combined or multi-endpoint error, `block_sigma`, M3 censoring, IOV,
`iiv_on_ruv`, FREM, custom residual magnitude, log-transform-both-sides,
mixtures, fixed residual SDs, and models with a free numerical structural theta
continue to use the general NLopt M-step.

#### The NLopt M-step (BOBYQA) {#saem-mstep-bobyqa}

The NLopt M-step uses **BOBYQA** (derivative-free trust-region with quadratic interpolation). The earlier gradient-based SLSQP path was found to lock onto one side of the Emax-Hill identifiability ridge on the dense-Emax PKPD benchmark (under-estimating EMAX by ~40% at virtually identical OFV); BOBYQA's quadratic trust-region exploration lands much closer to truth and ~40% faster on that benchmark (no FD-gradient eval per parameter), while remaining numerically equivalent (ΔOFV < 0.1) on simpler PK-only models.

When `mu_referencing = false`, the full NLopt M-step runs for all thetas as before.

#### The optimizer of the numerical M-step (`mstep_optimizer`) {#saem-mstep-optimizer}

##### The two solves {#saem-mstep-optimizer-solves}


The numerical θ/σ M-step minimises a sum of per-observation Gaussian negative
log-likelihoods at the iteration's frozen η (SAEM) or at importance-weighted samples
(IMP, IMPMAP). `mstep_optimizer = auto`, the default, runs `newton` wherever its scope
(below) holds and `bobyqa` elsewhere — and, in SAEM, `bobyqa` too when no θ is left to the
numerical solve (every θ is owned by a closed-form step: a σ-only solve), where BOBYQA's
evaluations are all served by the prediction memo (below) and Newton's fused pass is extra
work for no fewer evaluations. IMP and IMPMAP keep `newton` for a σ-only solve: their
BOBYQA keeps no memo, so there Newton's is the gain. It is a rule, not a request the model
can fail, so it is silent; the fit file records the result (`mstep_optimizer: newton` under `model`)
and `FitResult::mstep_optimizer_used` carries it (both are absent where SAEM runs no numerical solve at all: a single additive or proportional σ with every free θ mu-referenced is updated in closed form). BOBYQA reads only objective *values*: it
spends `2n + 1` of them on its first interpolation model and several more per step. The
same fit can instead read the exact derivatives, which the adjoint produces from one
recording of the predictions:

- `mstep_optimizer = newton` takes Fisher-scoring (Gauss-Newton) steps. One pass returns
  the objective, its exact score (the adjoint θ score and the analytic σ score) and the
  expected information `Σⱼ [∇fⱼ∇fⱼᵀ/Vⱼ + ½ ∇Vⱼ∇Vⱼᵀ/Vⱼ²]`, which is positive semi-definite. The
  step solves it from the previous M-step's point, Levenberg-damped where it does not
  factor or the objective rejects it, and a trial point is judged on the objective
  *value alone*: only an accepted point the solve continues from pays for the
  derivatives. It stops, as BOBYQA does, on NLopt's rule: a decrease below `1e-7` relative to
  the objective's size (the mean of the old and new values) or below `1e-7` absolute, so an
  objective near zero, or crossing it, does not collapse the tolerance to nothing — on an
  accepted plain Fisher step, and at any point on the decrease
  the *undamped* Fisher step predicts for it (a damping carried over from earlier
  rejections shortens a step, so a step at that damping understates what is left and never
  decides convergence) — within the evaluation budget BOBYQA gets (below), in which every
  pass, value or fused, counts as one evaluation. A warm-started M-step is typically one fused
  pass plus one or two value passes. The prediction alone never ends a solve before the
  objective has confirmed a step: a start the model calls converged still takes its one
  undamped Fisher step (one value pass) and the objective decides, as BOBYQA's first design
  always evaluates. Where the objective is dominated by a constant the model cannot see — a
  start at which a subject is scored by the invalid-variance guard carries 1e13 of it — the
  relative tolerance is the constant's, and a decrease of 0.08 predicted there is far inside
  it while the smooth part still has something to give. A start that is converged costs one
  value pass for it; measured over nine Newton fits (SAEM, IMP, IMPMAP; three seeds each) the
  confirmation changes whole-fit instructions by 0.97 to 1.00 times (SAEM 0.99 to 1.00, IMP and
  IMPMAP 0.97 to 0.99): it does not slow a fit.
- `mstep_optimizer = lbfgs` runs NLopt L-BFGS on the same score. It needs a gradient
  pass per iteration and has no curvature to start from (see the table); it is kept as
  the quasi-Newton alternative.

All three solve the same problem — same objective, packed space, bounds and tolerance — so
they move to the same optimum; they are not a different estimator. An explicit `newton` on
a model outside its scope still warns and runs `bobyqa`; `auto` does not.

##### Budget and scope {#saem-mstep-optimizer-budget}

BOBYQA runs to its tolerance (`1e-7` relative) wherever it runs: `bobyqa` itself, the
out-of-scope models under `auto`, and Newton's continuation. Its evaluation budget is a
runaway guard of 100 evaluations per interpolation point of its model (`2n + 1` points for
`n` free coordinates), not the `mstep_maxiter · (n + 1)` of a gradient method, which BOBYQA's
own first design (`2n + 1` evaluations) used up: with nine numerical θ nearly every M-step
stopped on that budget, far from the maximiser. The 100 is not tuned: it is 3 times the
largest need measured, and the stop-reason census below shows the guard binding on none of
the benchmark M-steps. `lbfgs` (a gradient method, `n + 1` evaluations per gradient) and
SAEM's mixture arm (which keeps its pre-#1415 configuration) keep `maxiter · (n + 1)`.

`newton` serves exactly the models whose expected information has a closed form from the
adjoint: the adjoint in scope, a plain Gaussian likelihood (no M3 censoring, TTE endpoint,
`block_sigma` residual correlation, `[covariate_nn]` θ or residual magnitude), and not a
mixture (SAEM, IMP and IMPMAP alike). IOV is inside it. This is decided once per fit; on any
other model the M-step runs `bobyqa`, and a warning in the fit's `warnings` names the
property that put the model out of scope. Fisher scoring is never run on finite-difference
curvature. A Newton solve that cannot take a step it has not converged for (information
that does not factor at any damping, or no damped step that decreases the objective)
continues with BOBYQA from the point it reached, with the evaluations Newton did not spend
(one budget per M-step), and the weighted M-step's failure and frozen-coordinate gates
(`W_MCEM_MSTEP_FAILED`, `W_MCEM_MSTEP_FROZEN`) see that continuation. So does a solve whose
information is unavailable at run time — a subject whose recording the adjoint declines
inside a model the scope decision admitted: the fit's `warnings` count the M-steps handed
to BOBYQA this way and the cause.

##### Measured {#saem-mstep-optimizer-measured}

Whole SAEM fits (150 + 250 iterations, `--threads 1`, instructions retired in user
space, median of five seeds). Every optimizer first benefits from the prediction memo
described next; the "before" column is the default solve without it.

| set | numerical M-step | BOBYQA before | BOBYQA | L-BFGS | Newton |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pk1` (500 subjects) | σ only | 26.79 G | **20.19** (1.33×) | 23.15 | 20.38 |
| `pk1_ode` | σ only | 78.95 | **40.37** (1.96×) | 43.32 | 40.52 |
| `pk1_sparse` | σ only | 10.72 | **8.20** (1.31×) | 9.13 | 8.54 |
| `pk2_big` (14 θ) | σ and 2 θ | 40.16 | **28.24** (1.42×) | 32.04 | 28.75 |
| `wiov` (IOV) | σ only | 82.37 | **60.31** (1.37×) | 64.49 | 61.13 |
| `corr` | none (all closed form) | 8.04 | 8.04 | 8.04 | 8.04 |

Without the memo (the first measurement of this option) Newton was 1.13 to 1.54 times
cheaper than BOBYQA, because BOBYQA's 8 to 15 value evaluations each predicted again and
Newton needs 3 to 4 passes. Predictions never depend on σ and a solve holds every η, κ and
importance sample fixed, so every evaluation at an unchanged θ shares one prediction pass
per subject (per sample): in a σ-only M-step that is every evaluation. The memo is kept only
where an evaluation can repeat a θ — a SAEM solve whose θ are all pinned (every evaluation)
and a Newton solve (the value pass at a trial point, then the fused pass at the accepted
one); a free-θ solve under BOBYQA or L-BFGS visits no θ twice and stores nothing. IMP and
IMPMAP keep it under `newton` and `lbfgs` only: their samples are `imp_samples` (1000 by default, up to
10 000 under auto-sampling) per subject, so the memo is `subjects × samples × n_obs`
numbers, several times what the estimator itself holds, and a default fit must not grow by
that. (Under `bobyqa` it would serve the σ-only solve on every evaluation and halve a
fit's instructions, 2.1× on the benchmarks, for 112 MB at 2000 subjects × 1000 samples × 7
observations; under the opt-in solvers the cost is the documented price of the option.) A sample takes
space only once it is scored (a zero importance weight takes none), and a subject's buffer grows
with the samples scored, never with the sample count. A Newton solve that stalls and hands over
to BOBYQA drops a memo that follows θ (free θ) first: BOBYQA evaluates each θ once, so
that memo could only copy predictions in and never serve one. A memo that holds a pinned θ
(a σ-only solve) is kept: the continuation sees the same θ bit for bit and every one of its
evaluations is a hit. The θ is
compared once per evaluation and a subject's samples share one buffer that a hit borrows.
It returns the predictions the solve's own predictor returned the first time,
so the fit file and the sdtab of all 90 fits (6 sets, 3 optimizers, 5 seeds) are
byte-identical to the memo-free run, and BOBYQA alone takes 1.3 to 2.0 times fewer
instructions. What is left of the M-step is one prediction pass plus residual arithmetic,
and there the optimizers are within 1 to 4 percent of each other (Newton slightly
behind). `newton` and `lbfgs` are therefore alternatives, not an optimization: reach for
`newton` where evaluations stay expensive (a free θ that moves every trial), not for speed
in a σ-only solve.

Same-seed estimates agree with BOBYQA's to well inside one standard error on every
parameter of `pk1`, `pk1_ode` and `wiov` (largest median difference 0.21 SE, largest single
seed 0.37 SE). `pk1_sparse` moves a typical value by up to 1.5 SE on one seed, with an
importance-sampled −2 log L within seed noise (BOBYQA 1415.0, Newton 1414.9 median).
On `pk2_big`, the 14-θ model whose SAEM fits spread widely from seed to seed, 15 seeds give an importance-sampled −2 log L of −3501.9 (median) under both BOBYQA and Newton, means −3501.0 and −3499.7 (standard deviations 4.3 and 5.8): not distinguishable at this sample size, with Newton's bad tail a little heavier (its worst seed is 13 units worse than BOBYQA's fit of the same seed).

Against NONMEM and the published references, the anchors that run a numerical M-step
(`warfarin_impmap`, `warfarin_imp`, `warfarin_iov_impmap`, `covmuref_power_saem`) land on
the same worst |z| under every optimizer to the six digits the fit file prints: with σ the
only numerical coordinate the solve is one-dimensional and every optimizer converges to
the same point, so identical anchor rows are the expected reading, not a sign that the
option did nothing (`mstep_optimizer` reaches the M-step on each of the three estimators,
the IOV score included; a unit test counts the solver that actually ran).

##### Newton as the default {#saem-mstep-default}

`mstep_optimizer = auto` (#3001) makes Newton the default M-step and BOBYQA run to its
tolerance the rule everywhere else. This changes default results. Measured against the
previous default (`bobyqa` on a `maxiter · (n + 1)` budget): seeds 1 and 2, `--threads 1`,
instructions retired in user space, importance-sampled −2 log L (`K = 20000`) at the final
estimates, so a negative difference is a better fit.

| model | numerical coordinates | instructions, new / old | −2 log L, new − old |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pk2_big_nomu` (SAEM) | 11 | 0.69 | −133.5, −128.6 |
| `warfarin_nomu` | 4 θ + σ | 0.75 | −25.0, −15.9 |
| `mm` (ODE) | 2 | 0.66 | −28.9, −21.4 |
| `anchor_a_nomu` | 9 | 0.51 | −2.4, −23.9 |
| `shared_nomu` | 8 | 0.57 | −5.0, −6.2 |
| `pk1_nomu` (5 seeds) | 5 | 0.68 | −1.5 to +2.9 |
| `imp_non_mu_ref` (IMP) | 14 θ | 0.23 | −1.5, −2.6 |
| IMPMAP, σ only (3 models) | 1 | 0.39 to 0.54 | 0.000 |
| SAEM, σ only (14 models) | 0 to 1 | 1.00 (`auto` is `bobyqa` there: the BOBYQA fit) | 0.000 |
| SAEM, 2 θ on an ODE model (`frac_ode`) | 3 | 1.14 | within ±1.3 |

The gain on the multi-θ models is mostly BOBYQA's old budget, not Newton: BOBYQA spends
`2n + 1` evaluations on its first design, so on nine numerical θ nearly every M-step stopped
on the budget far from the maximiser. Run to its tolerance (explicit `bobyqa` now) it
reaches the same −2 log L (−3501 against Newton's −3502 on a nine-θ model); Newton gets there in 0.5 to 0.7 times the instructions. Where
the M-step is σ only (a combined error with every θ mu-referenced), both solves are served by
the prediction memo — one prediction pass per M-step — and Newton's σ score and information
are residual arithmetic on it, no recording: the same cost per iteration (0 to 7 percent more
instructions on 14 SAEM models; 7.21 against 7.28 ms per iteration on the pk2_big stand-in).
But Newton's exact σ follows each draw's noise, where the warm-started BOBYQA, stopping at its
tolerance, smooths it, and the automatic exploration stop then fires later: on 30 pk2_big
seeds K1 had a median of 2110 against 1805 (longer on 18 seeds, shorter on 8), about 10 percent
more CPU at the same −2 log L. So SAEM's `auto` keeps `bobyqa` there and the fit is the BOBYQA
fit: identical estimates and instructions to `mstep_optimizer = bobyqa`. IMP and IMPMAP keep
`newton` for σ-only solves, where BOBYQA has no memo and Newton's is the gain (0.39 to 0.54
times). A model with a numerical θ stays on `newton`: `frac_ode`, an ODE model
with two θ that have no η, costs 1.14 times BOBYQA's instructions there.

Newton's M-step is as exact as BOBYQA's at the same tolerance. On `pk1_nomu`, `pk2_big`,
`warfarin_iov` and `wiov` (304 M-steps each) a converged reference solve from the same start
puts Newton's objective within 3.4e-4 of it at the worst M-step (median 4e-9 to 9e-6), against
0.14 for BOBYQA at its worst on `pk1_nomu`; in a one-coordinate σ solve BOBYQA is the tighter (median
1e-14 to 3e-12 against 4e-9 to 7e-7) and both are far inside the E-step's Monte Carlo noise. The census of
BOBYQA's stop reasons over the same fits finds `FtolReached` on every M-step of every
model but the mixture arm, at most 33 evaluations per interpolation point, so the 100 of the
runaway guard never binds.

The standing seed-to-seed spread decides what a paired difference means. Over 15 seeds
`warfarin_iov` gives −2 log L 310.75 (Newton), 310.72 (BOBYQA to tolerance) and 310.56
(previous default), standard deviation 0.5; the worst |z| of an ω against NONMEM is 8.1,
6.9 and 5.7 (the ω have a small NONMEM standard error, so the SAEM's own noise reads as
several z). `pk2_big` over 40 seeds gives −3489.4 (Newton, sd 14.7, median −3495.3) and −3488.5 (BOBYQA,
sd 11.3, median −3491.9), a paired difference of −0.9 ± 2.0: the same distribution, with two
Newton seeds beyond −3460 (−3443.9, −3448.3) against one for BOBYQA (−3459.3). Nothing in the
solve separates them. In the worst seed every one of the 304 Newton M-steps converged (none
stalled, handed over to BOBYQA, or converged at its start), and each agrees with BOBYQA's
solve from the same state to 1e-4 in log σ; the two fits decorrelate by M-step 10 to 20 from
that difference through the E-step's sampling, and end on different draws from one
multimodal SAEM distribution. This model's numerical M-step is σ only (two σ), so
`auto` runs `bobyqa` on it and the default does not see the tail at all.

NONMEM anchors that run a numerical M-step, worst |z| before to after (median of two
seeds): `warfarin_saem` SAEM 0.73 to 0.73 and IMPMAP 0.74 to 0.74, `warfarin_iov` IMPMAP 0.70
to 0.70, `imp_non_mu_ref` IMP 2.15 to 0.30, `warfarin_nomu` SAEM 17.4 to 4.2.

#### Thetas the closed-form update cannot reach {#saem-mstep-no-closed-form}

Two model shapes leave a theta on the numerical M-step. The first is slower; the second
can bias the estimate outright.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Non-mu-referenced parameters slow SAEM convergence

Whenever the estimation chain runs SAEM, ferx warns if any individual parameter's
random effect is **not** mu-referenced — for example
`BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_E0` when TVE0 is also read in `[structural_model]`, so it
does not enter only through that line
([additive mu-references](#saem-mstep-additive)). Such parameters cannot use the closed-form EM update
above and fall back to the slower NLopt M-step, which can strongly slow convergence.
(A typical value that reads several thetas, such as an additive covariate model, is
*not* in this class since #619 — see [covariate
mu-references](#saem-mstep-covariate-mu-ref).) The warning fires independently of the `mu_referencing`
fit option: turning the option off does not remove the risk — it removes the
mu-centering that mitigates it — so the diagnostic is most warranted in exactly that
case. Prefer log-mu-referenced forms (`P = TV * exp(ETA)`), the additive form
(`E0 = TVE0 + ETA_E0`, or a sum with one bare theta and one eta), or, for a parameter
bounded to $(0,1)$, the
logit-scale form `P = inv_logit(LOGIT_P + ETA_P)`.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## A theta with no ETA at all rides a different, noisier update

The warning above covers a parameter whose eta ferx could not mu-reference. A
**fixed-effect-only theta** — one that carries no eta anywhere in
`[individual_parameters]` — is a distinct case, and SAEM warns about it
separately:

```
SAEM: estimated parameter(s) [TVFRD1] have NO associated ETA, so they are not
mu-referenced and are moved only by the η-frozen numerical M-step. ...
```

Such a theta never receives the closed-form `log θ += γ·mean(η)` shift, which is
an exact Robbins-Monro average. Its only channel is the numerical M-step, which
re-maximises the conditional observation likelihood against each iteration's
MCMC η draw and assigns the maximiser. That is a valid stochastic-EM update —
its fixed point is the marginal optimum whenever the E-step samples the right
conditional — but it is noisier than the closed-form shift, it runs only every
third exploration iteration, and on a poorly mixing chain it can settle away
from the marginal optimum (see the FREM case below).

Before 0.4.x (#1415) this channel was broken in a way that read as "biased":
