the NLopt solve behind it started from a first design a quarter of the bound
range wide (×12–×26 of the current value on the default bounds) and stopped on
a `1e-4` relative tolerance, so it returned a few percent of a step; and #1011
had then blended even that at 3 % per exploration M-step. The result was a
theta that travelled a small fraction of the way to the optimum and stopped,
on every model with such a theta — allometric and maturation exponents,
covariate slopes, inter-compartmental clearances. Both are fixed: the solve
starts local and converges, and the exploration cap is off by default (it is
kept only for `iiv_on_ruv` models — see the next section).

Measured on the three `ferx-testdata` models of #1415, importance-sampled
−2 log L at the final estimates (lower is better; the IS readout, not the
FOCE approximation the fit YAML reports — see below):

| model (no-ETA thetas) | before | after | reference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| melphalan (`TVQ`, `CL_CRCL`) | 2705.8 | 2684.0 | NONMEM SAEM 2682.4 |
| clofarabine (`TVQ`, `TVV2`, `THALF`) | 17778.5 | 17764.3 | NONMEM SAEM 17734.6 |
| thiotepa (nine of eleven thetas) | 6047.8 | 5827.3 | IS at the FOCEI optimum 5823.6 |

On thiotepa every no-ETA theta had ended within a few percent of its initial
value; after the fix they land where FOCEI lands. The in-repo anchor is
`covmuref_power` with the weight covariate routed through a local assigned
before an `if` with no `else` and again in its arm, so the #619 group detection
does not apply and `TH_WT` rides this channel: NONMEM SAEM 0.921, ferx 0.332
before (its 0.3 start) and 0.961 after. (The fixture wrote a plain `if` / `else`
until [#1422](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1422) made that form
a group; the values it computes are unchanged.)

Two structural remedies remain better than this channel where they apply:

* **Attach an eta** — `P = TVP * exp(ETA_P)` with a small omega (optionally
  `FIX`). ferx then mu-references it automatically and the exact closed-form
  update takes over.
* **Write a covariate model in a form #619 can see** — a covariate read from
  the data directly or through a local, including one every arm of an
  `if` / `else` assigns, rather than one assigned in only some arms — so the
  slope joins the typical value's mu-reference group.

Otherwise cross-check against [FOCEI](foce.qmd) or [IMPMAP](impmap.qmd), which
do not depend on this channel.
:::

##### A theta whose eta the shift cannot use

The "NO associated ETA" advisory above lists only thetas that appear in no
statement with an eta. A theta that *does* share a parameter with an eta in a
form the shift cannot use, such as a Box-Cox
`CL = TVCL * exp((exp(ETA_CL)^LAMBDA - 1) / LAMBDA)` (`log CL` is not linear in
the eta) or a covariate coefficient no group owns, rides the same numerical
M-step but gets its own message (#1715): it "carries an ETA, but not as a
mu-referenced typical value". Keep the transform. Cross-check against
FOCEI/IMPMAP, or hold it `FIX`. IMP/IMPMAP and FREM conversion split the same way.

### Averaging a maximiser is not maximising the average {#saem-mstep-jensen}

The numerical M-step re-maximises the frozen-η objective against **one** draw and
then adopts that maximiser. A maximiser is a nonlinear function of the draw, so
what the run converges to is `E[θ*(η)]` rather than the `θ` that maximises
`E[Q(θ, η)]` — SAEM's actual target. The difference is a Jensen-type bias that
grows with the dispersion of the draws, which is why it gets *worse* when the
E-step samples better (#1458).

It is invisible in the trace: the objective is fine, and only a comparison
against a long-run reference or a FOCEI fit shows it. Two opt-in alternatives
attack it: one **removes** the Jensen term by never forming a maximiser, the
other **shrinks** it by averaging more draws into the one it forms. Both are
**off by default**, and a fit that sets neither is bit-identical to before.

#### The two alternatives

`mstep_solver = score_sa`
: Solves the score equation `E[∇Q(x, η)] = 0` by stochastic approximation,
  preconditioned by the SA-averaged expected information (Kuhn & Lavielle 2005):

  ```
  I_k = (1 − γ_k)·I_{k−1} + γ_k·I(x_k, η_k)
  x_{k+1} = x_k − γ_k·(I_k + λ·diag I_k)⁻¹·∇Q(x_k, η_k)
  ```

  A fixed point needs `E[∇Q(x*, η)] = 0`, which is the stationarity condition of
  the averaged objective, so no Jensen term arises. σ takes the same Newton
  *direction* as every other coordinate, but the step gives it a **target** that
  `damp_mstep_sigma_variance` then moves it a `γ_σ = min(γ, 0.2, γ_mstep)`
  fraction of the way to, on the variance scale — the same
  [#1445](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1445) policy the
  derivative-free arms use, not a second copy of it. That is a smaller *gain* on
  the step, not the blend stacked on top of it (which really would move σ at
  `γ²`). One gradient sweep is cheaper than the population passes a derivative-free
  solve run to its tolerance costs (tens to hundreds of value evaluations per M-step), so this M-step runs every iteration
  rather than every third during exploration. The score's θ block, and the
  per-observation `∂f/∂θ` the expected information is built from, are exact: one
  recording of the subject's predictions with θ on the adjoint's tape and one
  reverse sweep, whatever the number of θ, in place of a forward difference per θ.
  A model outside the adjoint recorder's scope keeps the forward difference.

`mstep_draws = K`
: Averages the *derivative-free* M-step objective over this iteration's η draw
  and the previous `K − 1` iterations' draws, so the maximiser NLopt returns is
  the maximiser of an average. The bias falls roughly as `1/K` — it shrinks, it
  does not go away — at `K` times the M-step's objective evaluations, and only to
  the extent that consecutive draws decorrelate, which under the default sticky
  random-walk E-step they largely do not. Ignored under `score_sa`.

Both are restricted to the plain Gaussian residual scope the expected
information has a closed form on: no IOV, no [mixture](mixture.qmd), no M3, no
time-to-event endpoint, no `block_sigma` residual correlation, no
`[covariate_nn]` θ, no residual magnitude. FREM is in scope since #1421, which
fixed the σ score of its covariate pseudo-observations. A model outside it keeps
the historical solver and says so by name in the fit's warnings.

#### Measured

On the busulfan benchmark of #1458 (`ferx-testdata/busulfan_dominic`, 600
subjects, analytic 2-cpt IV, `block_omega(ETA_CL, ETA_V1)` + `omega ETA_V2`, combined
error, `TVQ` with no ETA), 6 seeds at the default 150/250/20 schedule, on the
importance-sampled −2 log L — the neutral readout, since a SAEM fit has no objective of
its own. `B6qfix` is the same model with `TVQ` held `FIX`, which removes this channel and
nothing else:

| | `TVQ` free | `TVQ` FIX | what a free no-ETA θ costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| default (`bobyqa`) | 60044.87 ± 3.29 | 60035.12 ± 2.08 | **+9.75** |
| `mstep_solver = score_sa` | 60034.59 ± 5.27 | 60031.22 ± 3.35 | **+3.37** |
| `mstep_draws = 2` | 60043.87 ± 3.77 | 60034.62 ± 3.45 | +9.25 |
| `mstep_draws = 3` | 60045.61 ± 2.36 | 60033.99 ± 3.50 | +11.62 |

`score_sa` removes about two-thirds of the penalty, at the same cost (6.40 against 6.47
CPU-seconds: one gradient sweep every iteration in place of a derivative-free solve every
third). `mstep_draws` does not move it at all here and costs 53 % (`K = 2`) to 89 %
(`K = 3`) more CPU — consecutive draws of the default random-walk E-step are too
correlated for a two- or three-draw average to be worth anything, which is the regime
#1458 predicted it would fail in. It is kept because that argument is about the *kernel*,
not about the estimator, and a near-i.i.d. kernel changes it.

On the 100-subject subset the three arms are a tie (7531.37 ± 0.37 default against
7531.14 ± 0.93 for `score_sa`), with `score_sa`'s seed spread 2.5× wider.

#### Why `score_sa` is not the default

It was a candidate in [#1449](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1449) and it
is not a close call on either side, which is why the answer is worth recording.

**For.** Re-measured at today's shipped defaults (`n_mh_steps = auto`) over all eight
SAEM benchmarks, 6 seeds each, single-threaded, it is tie-or-better than `bobyqa` on the
importance-sampled −2 log L on every one — best on busulfan (−5.14), busulfan-`TVQ`-FIX
(−5.58) and the thiotepa ODE bench (−11.07) — and it costs **25–54 % less CPU** (cefepime
5.36 → 2.45 s, thiotepa 215 → 94 s), because one gradient sweep per iteration replaces a
derivative-free solve whose cost is the population passes of a BOBYQA solve run to its
tolerance (tens to hundreds of value evaluations per M-step).

**Against — the σ half, fixed in
[#1480](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1480).** As #1458 shipped it,
`score_sa` stepped σ at the shared γ and in packed (log σ) units, which is #1445's two
defects at once: during exploration `γ = 1`, so that is a *full* Newton step to one
draw's score root with no Robbins-Monro averaging, and a log-scale blend is a geometric
mean of the σ sequence. On the sparse combined-error fixture of #1445 — 300 subjects
with a median of one observation each, truth `combined(prop = 0.13, add = 1.8)` — it
scattered the *minority* additive σ. Measured seeds 1 / 2 / 3, `ci-test`, aarch64:

| | `ADD_ERR` (truth 1.8) | cross-seed sd |
|---|---|---|
| `bobyqa` (the default) | 1.33 / 1.83 / 2.17 | 0.42 |
| `score_sa` as #1458 shipped it | **0.84 / 0.52 / 1.13** | 0.31 |
| `score_sa` with the γ_σ schedule only | 0.87 / 0.99 / 1.20 | 0.17 |
| `score_sa` after #1480 | 1.90 / 1.86 / 2.11 | 0.14 |

The third row is why the fix is both halves: the schedule alone still leaves seed 1 at
0.87, under the factor-of-two gate of 0.9. The objective could not see any of it — the
FOCE readout differs by under 2 units across all those fits, and the benchmark suite's
−2 log L prefers `score_sa` throughout. This is the same channel #1445 is about, a
variance component identified only where `σ_add` and `σ_prop·f` are comparable, and it
is why `tests/saem_combined_error.rs` scores it against **simulation truth** rather than
against another estimator.

**Against — the θ half, still open (#1480).** On the #619 `covmuref_power` anchor, whose
`TH_WT` anchors no mu-reference and therefore moves only through this channel, `score_sa` at the
default 150/250 schedule reaches **0.746** against NONMEM SAEM's 0.921 — outside the
0.12 window the default solver satisfies. It is slow rather than wrong: at 300/700 it
lands at **0.9845** (|Δ| 0.063) while `bobyqa` at that same schedule *overshoots* to
1.1485 (|Δ| 0.227). So the window is a property of the estimator and the schedule
together, and `score_sa` needs a longer run on a θ that starts far from its optimum.
`tests/saem_covariate_mu_ref.rs` keeps the anchor at 300/700 live and gates the
default-schedule arm on the open issue.

A default has to be safe for the parameter the likelihood barely constrains and has to
converge in the schedule it ships with, so `score_sa` stays opt-in. It is worth reaching
for on a model with a free θ that has no ETA, with a longer schedule than the default if
that θ starts far away.

One further thing #1449 measured: `score_sa`'s score/information sweep does not reuse the
cached event schedule, so on a model whose `[individual_parameters]` read `TIME` or a
time-varying covariate it rebuilds two schedules per subject per iteration. That is an
unrealised saving on top of the CPU numbers above, not a regression against them.

Two things the numbers do **not** say. First, `d_final` against a long-run reference gets
*worse* under `score_sa` (`TVQ` moves from −0.04 to −0.18 log units away from it) — but
that reference is the same estimator run longer, so it carries the same bias, and it
cannot arbitrate a change that removes it. Second, a FOCEI fit of the same model is not
the oracle either: its own importance-sampled −2 log L is 60046.43, worse than every SAEM
arm above, so it locates `TVQ` (7.60) no better than they do.

::: {.callout-note}
## Neither is a substitute for attaching an ETA

A θ that carries a random effect gets the exact closed-form Robbins-Monro shift
and never enters this channel at all. Both options above make the numerical
channel unbiased in the limit; the closed form is exact at every iteration. Where
the model can be written so #619's [covariate
mu-references](#saem-mstep-covariate-mu-ref) apply, that remains the better fix.
:::

### The exploration cap (`mstep_damping`) is a hold, not a cure {#what-saem-does-about-it-now}

`mstep_damping` blends the numerical M-step result in as
`θ ← θ + γ_θ·(θ* − θ)` during exploration, with `γ_θ` capped at the value
you set, and averages it at `γ = 1/(k−k1)` in convergence. **It is off by
default** (`1.0`, plain assignment in both phases) for every model except one
with `iiv_on_ruv`, which keeps the 0.03 cap — the reason is measured below:

```
[fit_options]
  method        = saem
  mstep_damping = 0.03   # opt in: hold the no-ETA thetas near their start
```

It was introduced by #1011 at a default of 0.03 after a FREM `iiv_on_ruv` model
(475 subjects, 12 etas) whose absorption-split fraction `TVFRD1`
(`D1 = MAT*(1-TVFRD1)`, `KA = 1/(MAT*TVFRD1)`, no eta of its own) drifted from
0.383 to 0.039 under the undamped update, while IMP (0.311), IMPMAP (0.318)
and NONMEM IMP (0.394) agree. The capped fit ended at 0.29–0.36, which read as
"landing on the marginal optimum". #1415 measured what the cap does, with the
M-step solver repaired:

* **It holds the theta where it starts.** On the same reprex: 0.383 → 0.361,
  and from a deliberately wrong 0.2 start, 0.2 → 0.191. Its good answer was
  the model's initial estimate, which that auto-generated model had taken from
  a FOCEI fit.
* **It freezes every other no-ETA theta the same way**, because the cap
  divides the number of EM steps the exploration phase amounts to (50 M-steps
  × cap), and a covariate slope confounded with an eta needs all of them.
  `covmuref_power` `TH_WT` (NONMEM 0.921, start 0.3): cap 0.03 → 0.323,
  0.1 → 0.340, 0.3 → 0.403, off → 0.961. Thiotepa (IS −2 log L, optimum
  5824): 0.03 → 5928, 0.1 → 5897, 0.3 → 5860, off → 5827.
* **The convergence-phase Robbins-Monro average hurts too.** `γ = 1/(k−k1)`
  is the right average for a statistic that is stationary around the optimum,
  but the sequence of η-frozen maximisers is an EM trajectory, so averaging it
  weights the early, still-crawling iterates most (`TH_WT` 0.637 with the
  average, 0.961 without).

#### Why the default is keyed to `iiv_on_ruv`

The FREM drift itself is real and is **not** fixed: undamped, that reprex
settles near `TVFRD1` 0.15–0.18 from either start on the default schedule,
keeps drifting on a 3× longer one (0.03), and 200 MH steps per iteration do
not change it — so it is not plain E-step under-mixing. The importance-sampled
objective ranks the drifted point worse, by 7–11 units — see [what #1421
measured](#saem-1421-measured) below, which also shows that the FOCEI
objective first used for this ranking is not a reliable one on an
`iiv_on_ruv` model.

It needs **both `iiv_on_ruv` and FREM**. The same model with its `iiv_on_ruv`
line and `ETA_RUV` omega removed lands undamped at `TVFRD1` 0.414, `TVMAT`
2.680, `TVV` 137.6 — on NONMEM IMP's 0.394 / 2.680 / 133.8 — where the 0.03
cap leaves it at 0.342 / 2.228 / 147.5. With `iiv_on_ruv` but without the FREM
covariate rows, every SAEM variant lands somewhere the objective cannot tell
from the optimum. So **the default is keyed to `iiv_on_ruv`**: such a model
keeps the 0.03 cap, every other model runs undamped, and a value you set wins
either way. It is keyed to `iiv_on_ruv` alone, not to `iiv_on_ruv` *with*
FREM, because that one non-FREM measurement cannot tell the cap from the
undamped update: `TVFRD1` is barely identified there, so it shows the cap is
harmless on that data, not that undamped is safe on a non-FREM `iiv_on_ruv`
model whose no-ETA thetas are identified. If yours is such a model, set
`mstep_damping = 1.0` and compare the two fits by importance sampling (see
[below](#saem-1421-measured)). `FIX` is the honest spelling of the same hold
when the value is known.

#### Which fits it damps

The option only acts on the channel it is about: a fit is damped when NLopt is
left estimating a theta that is **not mu-referenced**, which is exactly the
situation the advisory above warns about. A theta that is `FIX`, that is
pinned out by the mu-reference shift, or that is mu-referenceable at all is
left on the undamped update, and setting `mstep_damping` on a model where no
theta trips the gate warns that it has no effect rather than accepting it
silently. **Sigma takes the same step as theta** when the cap applies, because
the numerical M-step is a single NLopt problem over `[θ; σ]` and a partial step
on one component alone would be inconsistent. Under `mu_referencing = false` a
theta written in a mu-referenceable form is not this channel either, so such a
fit keeps the undamped update and the option reports no effect.

[Mixture models](mixture.qmd) are excluded outright. A log-mu-referenced
`MIXNUM`-switched typical value takes the closed-form shift (without IOV,
#2458), but one without an orbit move (no mu-ref pair, `mu_referencing =
false`, or IOV) goes through the same numerical M-step, where its class typical
values must *separate* from a common start, and damping that excursion stalls
the separation. The mixture arm also keeps the pre-#1415 M-step solver
configuration. On the NONMEM-anchored mixture seed sweep it no longer changes
the answer (the switched θ there are closed-form), and for the mixtures without
an orbit move no configuration has been anchored yet.

#### What #1421 measured {#saem-1421-measured}

On the #1011 reprex (`n_exploration = 1000`, `n_convergence = 1000`,
`n_mh_steps = 50`, seed 12345), ranked by the importance-sampled −2 log L at
K = 20000 with the covariate etas Rao-Blackwellised (`frem_rao_blackwell`, the
default), evaluated at each point with `imp_eval_only`:

| point | `TVFRD1` | IS −2 log L |
|---|---:|---:|
| IMPMAP | 0.318 | 6857.1 ± 1.8 |
| SAEM, `mstep_solver = score_sa`, undamped | 0.147 | 6864.4 ± 1.4 |
| the same, 3× schedule (3000 + 2000) | 0.063 | 6868.2 ± 1.6 |
| IMPMAP with only `TVFRD1` moved to 0.15 | 0.150 | 6867.3 ± 1.6 |

At K = 5000 the undamped `bobyqa` point (0.149) scores 6866.7 ± 1.9 against
IMPMAP's 6856.0 ± 2.6; the order does not change with K. So on the FREM model
the drift moves away from the marginal optimum, and keeps moving on a longer
schedule. Every mechanism #1421 suggested was tested and **ruled out**, each by
one run that changes it alone:

* **η_RUV re-centring (#904)** — disabled, undamped still lands at 0.183.
* **Ω feedback** — the 11-eta FREM block held `FIX` at IMPMAP's Ω, undamped
  `bobyqa` still lands at 0.148 (0.149 with Ω free); `score_sa` at 0.230.
* **σ** — it reaches IMPMAP's 0.18 by iteration 5 and stays there.
* **The single-draw Jensen bias** — `score_sa`, which has no Jensen term, drifts
  too (the table above).
* **Declaration order** — `ETA_RUV` declared after the FREM block: 0.080.

The same data without the FREM covariate rows (the PK block of 3 plus
`ETA_RUV`, same schedule) shows no defect to fix: `bobyqa` undamped 0.242,
`score_sa` 0.401, the 0.03 hold 0.359, and from a 0.2 start 0.229 (hold) and
0.247 (`score_sa`) all score between −2276.8 and −2272.0 (MC SE 1.0–2.5) —
`TVFRD1` is barely identified there, and no SAEM variant is distinguishable from
another. What remains of #1421 is therefore the interaction of FREM's
covariate rows with `iiv_on_ruv`, and the hold stays the default for it.

#### The FOCEI objective cannot rank `iiv_on_ruv` fits

#1415 ranked the reprex's drifted and held points by the FOCEI objective at
each (47 units apart). That objective is not reliable at `ω_RUV ≈ 0.3`. On a
covariate-conditional twin of the reprex — the FREM block replaced by the
regression of the PK etas on the covariates implied by IMPMAP's Ω, so the
covariates enter as fixed effects and IS needs no Rao-Blackwellisation — the
FOCEI objective sits ~440 units from the IS −2 log L at every point, and it
carries a slope in `TVFRD1` that the marginal likelihood does not. Moving
`TVFRD1` alone at the IMPMAP point:

| `TVFRD1` | FOCEI objective | IS −2 log L (K = 20000) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.18 | −1950.7 | −2394.6 ± 1.4 |
| 0.28 | −1961.4 | −2396.8 ± 1.2 |
| 0.35 | −1965.9 | −2394.1 ± 1.2 |

FOCEI prefers the larger value by 15 units; IS is flat to within its noise. At
the fitted points the two disagree on the *sign*: FOCEI puts the `score_sa` fit
(0.184) 13.5 units behind IMPMAP's (0.279), IS puts it 3.2 ± 2.4 ahead. The
same holds for a FOCEI *fit*: on the no-FREM model above it estimates
`TVFRD1` 0.413 but `ω_RUV` 0.058 against SAEM's 0.28, and scores 124–129 units
worse than every SAEM point on the IS −2 log L (−2148.2 ± 0.2). Rank `iiv_on_ruv` fits by IS, as the
next section recommends for SAEM in general.

### Comparing a SAEM fit to FOCEI: read the importance-sampled objective

The `ofv` a SAEM fit reports is the FOCE approximation at the final estimates —
SAEM has no objective of its own — and until 0.4.x (#1415) a method *chain*
such as `method = [saem, imp]` computed it **without** the η–ε interaction,
while `method = saem` alone and every FOCEI fit computed it with. On the
thiotepa model that is a 175-unit difference at the same estimates, and it was
the bulk of the "SAEM is 341 units worse than FOCEI" that #1415 reported. A
chain now keeps the interaction flag unless its final stage is `foce`, as the
single-method form always did. When you compare estimators, compare the
importance-sampled −2 log L that an `imp_eval_only` stage prints (`IS done.
−2 log L = …`) or `FitResult::importance_sampling`, evaluated at each fit's
estimates.

### One seed cannot compare two builds {#saem-seed-spread}

SAEM is deterministic at a fixed `seed`: the same binary, model and data give the
same estimates to the last digit. A different ferx version can still give a
different number at that seed, because almost any change on the chain's path
(an extra random draw, a reordered update) sends it down another trajectory. On
the public stand-ins built for
[#2602](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2602) (450 subjects each:
a two-compartment oral closed form with a block Ω, and the same model as a
3-state ODE), `method = [saem, imp]` with `imp_eval_only = true` was run over 40 seeds. The IS −2 log L had a
seed-to-seed sd of 1.5 and 3.4–4.1, and a range of 7 and 14–15. The
importance-sampling draw alone, with the SAEM seed held fixed, accounts for an
sd of only 0.55 and 0.9. Most of the spread is where the chain ends. So a +4 or
+7 between two builds at one seed is not evidence of a regression. Between the
September build `e4743847` and `e1a05d1a`, the per-seed differences over the 40
seeds averaged −0.05 ± 0.26 and +0.31 ± 0.66 (mean ± SE).

To compare two builds, compare distributions:

```bash
tools/saem-seed-sweep.sh --model m.ferx --data d.csv \
  --rev e4743847 --rev main --seeds "$(seq -s ' ' 1 10)"
```

The script builds each revision and runs the model once per seed, with
`imp_seed = seed + 1000`. It replaces `seed`, its alias `saem_seed` and
`imp_seed` in `[fit_options]`. It prints each build's mean and sd, and the shift
against the first build. The shift is the mean of the per-seed differences, with
its standard error. Every build runs the same seed pairs, so pairing is the right
test. The model must end in an
`imp_eval_only` stage. `--fixed-saem-seed` varies only the IS draw, to measure
the Monte-Carlo noise floor by itself.

The number of NLopt evaluations saved is stored in `FitResult::saem_mu_ref_m_step_evals_saved`, accumulated across SAEM iterations as `2 × mstep_maxiter × n_mu_ref_pairs` per outer step (one finite-difference probe pair per pinned mu-ref dimension, capped at `mstep_maxiter` NLopt gradient requests). The field is `None` when mu-referencing is off or method ≠ SAEM.

When `n_leapfrog > 0`, `FitResult::saem_n_subjects_hmc` records how many subjects used HMC at least once during the E-step (the remainder used MH fallback). The field is `None` for MH-only runs. The fit YAML also emits `saem_n_subjects_hmc` and `saem_n_subjects_mh` when the field is `Some`.

### 5. Adaptive Step Sizes

The per-subject step scales $\delta_i$ (MH) and leapfrog step sizes (HMC) are
adapted toward a target acceptance rate. Which rule does the adapting is set by
`[fit_options] scale_adaptation`.

Target acceptance rates: 40% for the primary block kernel (MH or HMC's own 65%
when `n_leapfrog > 0`), 44% for the componentwise kernel. The block kernel and
the componentwise kernel carry independent per-subject scales, and each η's
componentwise scale is adapted separately.

#### `scale_adaptation = interval`

Every `adapt_interval` iterations, from that window's acceptance rate:

- above target: increase $\delta_i$ by 10% (up to 5.0)
- at or below target: decrease $\delta_i$ by 10% (down to 0.01, or 1e-6 for a
  componentwise scale)

**Know its reach.** The factor is fixed, so the total movement available is
`1.1^n` up or `0.9^n` down over the `n` times the rule fires — and on the
default 150 + 250 = 400 iterations at `adapt_interval = 50` that is **8** times,
i.e. at most ≈2.1× up or ≈0.43× down *however far from target the chain is*. A
model whose optimal step is an order of magnitude below the 0.3 starting value
never reaches it. `examples/warfarin_saem.ferx` is such a model: on the default
settings its combined acceptance collapses to 1.6% by iteration 26 and sits at
2–4% for the remaining ~375 iterations against the 40% target (issue #1444).

#### `scale_adaptation = robbins_monro` (default)

A Robbins–Monro step taken **every** iteration, from that iteration's own rate:

$$\log \delta_i \leftarrow \log \delta_i + c \, k^{-0.6} \, (\hat{a}_k - a^\ast)$$

with $c = 1$, $k$ the 1-based iteration, $\hat{a}_k$ the realised rate and
$a^\ast$ the target. The correction is proportional to the discrepancy, so the
reach is unlimited, and the $k^{-0.6}$ decay is the diminishing-adaptation
condition that keeps an adapting chain valid (Roberts & Rosenthal 2007). The
clamps are the same as the interval rule's.

**It is the default since #1449, and it was not always a free win.** What ferx
measures directly is the acceptance rate, and on `examples/warfarin_saem.ferx` at its shipped settings
(150 + 250 iterations, `n_mh_steps = 20`, seed 12345) the combined rate over
the last 100 iterations goes from **3.90%** under `interval` to **42.05%**
under `robbins_monro`, against the 40% target. That much is reproduced by
`tests/saem_scale_adaptation.rs`.

Whether a rate at target makes the *estimates* better is a separate question,
and one this page does not answer from its own runs. The SAEM benchmarking in
[issue #1444](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1444) reported, over
6 seeds on real datasets, that Robbins–Monro roughly halves warfarin's
final-estimate error against a long-run reference, changes little on models
whose baseline scale is already near target, and **regressed** pembrolizumab
(303 subjects, 4 η) — a model whose acceptance was already *above* target — by
+4.7 on the importance-sampled −2 log L. That regression is what kept the rule
opt-in.

It is gone at today's defaults, and the reason is worth knowing: those
measurements were taken at a fixed `n_mh_steps = 20`, and #1468 made the
proposal count `auto`, which resolves to **6** on that model. Re-measured at
the shipped defaults over 6 seeds ([#1449](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/1449)),
Robbins–Monro *improves* pembrolizumab by **−4.7**, and the only bench it costs
anything on is vancomycin (+0.98 against a 0.94 cross-seed sd) — which the dead
band below removes. #1444's own data already pointed this way: at
`n_mh_steps = 8` it won on that bench too. These numbers have no NONMEM
counterpart (NONMEM's SAEM exposes no comparable step-scale knob).

`scale_adaptation = interval` restores the historical rule exactly.

The κ (IOV) scales stay on the interval rule under both settings: the
per-occasion kernel makes one proposal per occasion per iteration, so a single
iteration's rate for one subject is a ratio of small integers, and the
Robbins–Monro arm has not been measured there.

#### `scale_deadband` — only correct a chain that is off target

`[fit_options] scale_deadband = <lo>,<hi>`, **default `0.15,0.60`**, makes the
Robbins–Monro step conditional: it fires only when that iteration's acceptance
is **outside** `[lo, hi]`, and inside the band the scale is left bit-for-bit
alone (there is no interval bump underneath it — the interval rule is off for
the whole run under `robbins_monro`). The band is one absolute acceptance
window shared by the block kernel (target 40%) and each componentwise
coordinate (44%). It is ignored under `scale_adaptation = interval`, which has
no per-iteration step to skip.

It exists for the failure the previous section names: the models Robbins–Monro
was written for sit at 2–4%, and the one it regressed was already *above*
target and got pulled down onto it.

**What it does, measured, is not quite what it was built for.** Over the
8-benchmark, 6-seed suite of #1449 the band turns the unbanded rule's one loss
into a win (vancomycin +0.98 → −0.13 on the importance-sampled −2 log L,
against a 0.94 cross-seed sd) and keeps most of its gains (pembrolizumab −4.69
→ −3.74, warfarin's rescue intact: tail acceptance 0.041 under `interval`,
0.422 unbanded, 0.391 banded). But it does **not** leave a near-target chain
alone: the realised tail acceptance is *lower* under the band than without it
on every bench measured, because of the fixed-point shift described below. The
improvement is real; the mechanism is not "the controller declined to act".

Two things to know before setting one:

- **A wide band freezes the scales; it does not disable the dead band.** The
  rule fires only outside the band, so a band wider than the spread of the
  per-iteration rate means no step ever runs. `scale_deadband = none` (or an
  empty band, `lo == hi`) is the spelling that restores plain Robbins–Monro,
  and a band covering all of `[0, 1]` is rejected with that message rather
  than accepted.
- **Setting it from Rust is validated too.** `FitOptions::saem_scale_deadband`
  is public, so a band can reach the sampler without passing the model-file
  parser. An empty, reversed, out-of-range or everything-covering band is
  dropped there — the fit runs the unbanded Robbins-Monro rule and says so in
  its warnings — so the two front ends cannot produce different numerical
  behaviour for the same option, and neither can freeze the step scales.

- **A band moves the fixed point.** A per-iteration rate is `n_accepted /
  n_proposals`, so it is quantised to multiples of `1/n_mh_steps` (block) or
  `1/n_cw_sweeps` (componentwise), and the band censors the small deviations
  while keeping the tails. Unless the band is symmetric about the target *and*
  the rate's distribution is symmetric, the surviving steps do not cancel at
  the target: the scale settles where the censored deviations balance, which is
  not where the unbanded rule settles. With the shipped band and
  `n_mh_steps = 6` that equilibrium is near 33% rather than 40%.

#### Acceptance-rate diagnostics

Two warnings land in `FitResult.warnings` (never on stderr), most severe first:

- **Not mixing** — the cumulative post-burn-in acceptance is below 1%. The
  sampled ETAs barely moved, so the M-step ran on degenerate sufficient
  statistics and Ω/σ are unreliable.
The realised tail rate is also available as `FitResult::saem_mh_accept_tail`,
so a script can check mixing without matching on the warning text.

- **Persistently far from target** — the acceptance over the **last 100**
  post-burn-in iterations is outside 10–80%. The band is deliberately wide: a
  fit at 0.25 or 0.60 is unremarkable, and this is not a range of "good" rates
  but the range outside which the step scales have demonstrably failed to find
  their target. The message carries the realised tail rate, the target, the
  window length and the cumulative rate, so you do not have to re-run with
  `optimizer_trace` to see how far off it was. It is the *tail* rather than the
  whole-run average that is reported, because a run that mixes badly early and
  recovers averages to a number describing neither half; and it stays quiet for
  runs with fewer than 25 post-burn-in iterations, where the realised rate
  describes the starting scale rather than a failure to reach target.

## Post-SAEM Finalization

After the SAEM iterations complete:

1. **EBE Refinement**: Run the standard FOCE inner loop (BFGS optimization) warm-started from the SAEM ETAs to obtain final empirical Bayes estimates
2. **Combined-error additive-collapse report**: for `combined(PROP, ADD)`
   residual-error models, when SAEM has left a *free* additive component `ADD`
   at or below `1e-3` — the detection band just above its `exp(-8) ≈ 3.35e-4`
   optimizer lower bound — the fit carries a warning saying so. It is a report, not a repair — ferx once ran a FOCEI
   marginal-likelihood polish here and adopted it if it lowered the OFV, and
   that silent second fit was removed in favour of the warning. The channel it
   was papering over is fixed at source: the σ M-step now takes a
   [damped σ step](#stochastic-approximation-update) instead of assigning a
   single draw's maximiser (issue #1445), so the collapse it guarded against no
   longer happens on a `combined()` model whose additive term is identified.
   The warning remains, because an additive term that genuinely is *not*
   identified in the data will still land on the bound and you should see that:
   check it yourself (RSE, σ-correlation, profile likelihood), and on sparse
   data prefer the importance-sampling −2LL over the Laplace OFV when judging
   whether the additive term is real.
3. **Reported OFV**: Report NONMEM's SAEM objective (`SAEMOBJ`, `saem_ofv = saem`, the default; not a likelihood) at the final estimates as `ofv`. The importance-sampled `−2 log L` (NONMEM `$EST METHOD=IMP EONLY=1`, `saem_ofv = imp`) is the explicit follow-up. There is no AIC or BIC for it (`aic` / `bic` are `None` / `null`, as NONMEM reports none); the FOCE/Laplace objective at the same estimates is kept as a separately labelled diagnostic (see [The reported OFV](#saem-reported-ofv))
4. **Covariance Step**: Optionally compute standard errors via the covariance step's Hessian (same method as FOCE: the exact R matrix in scope, the finite-difference stencil outside it) — on the FOCEI objective for an all-Gaussian model, and on the quadrature marginal when the model has a non-Gaussian endpoint (see [below](#saem-covariance-non-gaussian))
5. **Diagnostics**: Compute PRED, IPRED, CWRES, IWRES for each subject

### The reported OFV {#saem-reported-ofv}

SAEM maximises the exact marginal likelihood but produces no usable value of it. NONMEM
reports its **`SAEMOBJ`** for the SAEM step, a stochastic-approximation readout of the
complete-data objective that is *not a likelihood*, and follows `METHOD=SAEM` with
`METHOD=IMP EONLY=1` when the marginal `−2 log L` is wanted. ferx does the same: the `ofv` of a
SAEM fit is the SAEM objective, and the importance-sampled `−2 log L` is the explicit follow-up
(`saem_ofv = imp`, or `method = [saem, imp]` with `imp_eval_only = true`). **Do not compare the
SAEM objective across models or with a FOCE/FOCEI/IMP objective**: it is −2210 on the shared-θ
anchor where the exact marginal is −1199. AIC and BIC are therefore absent under the default
(`FitResult::aic` / `bic` are `None`, `aic: null` in `fit.yaml`; model search and the other
ranking tools stop with an error naming `saem_ofv = imp`). Set `saem_ofv = imp`, `agq` or
`focei` for information criteria, built from that likelihood value; rank models by the
importance-sampled objective (see
[the `iiv_on_ruv` example](importance-sampling.qmd#adaptive-evaluation) for why the Laplace value
is biased where SAEM is usually chosen).

```
[fit_options]
  method           = saem
  saem_ofv         = saem    # saem (default) | imp | agq | focei
  saem_ofv_samples = 3000    # importance samples per subject, saem_ofv = imp
  saem_ofv_nodes   = 11      # nodes per random effect, saem_ofv = agq
```

| `saem_ofv` | `ofv` | AIC, BIC | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `saem` (default) | NONMEM's `SAEMOBJ` | none (`None`) | Free (accumulated from the E-step's draws). IOV models (an IOV-only model included) average the joint density of data, η and κ draws; a model with no random effects at all reports the data `−2 log L`. A mixture has no NONMEM-anchored convention, so it reports the `imp` value **with a warning** naming the fallback. |
| `imp` | importance-sampled `−2 log L`, NONMEM `IMP EONLY=1` | from `ofv` | `saem_ofv_samples` draws per subject (3000, the `ISAMPLE=3000` setting the [NONMEM comparison](importance-sampling.qmd#nonmem-comparison) uses), seeded by `imp_seed` so two runs agree to the bit. Carries a Monte-Carlo standard error. |
| `agq` | adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature at the final estimates | from `ofv` | Deterministic and exact up to the node count; `saem_ofv_nodes ^ n_eta` evaluations per subject, so up to three random effects. A mixture, a model with more random effects, or an IOV model whose stacked grid (`n_eta + n_occ·n_kappa` dimensions) exceeds the quadrature grid limit falls back to `imp` with a warning. A natural cross-check of the IS value. |
| `focei` | the FOCE/Laplace objective | from `ofv` | The behaviour before #2973, and the value that is directly comparable with a FOCE/FOCEI fit. |

#### What the SAEM objective is {#saem-objective-definition}

$$\text{SAEMOBJ} = \sum_i -2\log\Big(\tfrac1K\sum_k p(y_i,\eta_{ik}\mid\theta,\Omega,\sigma)\Big)$$

the joint density of the data and the random effects, **no `2π` constants** (neither
`N_obs·log 2π` nor `NIND·NETA·log 2π`; `log|Ω|` and `log σ²` are in), averaged *inside* the log.
During burn-in the average runs over the chain states of the current iteration; in the
accumulation phase over the draws **and the iterations**, which is the value NONMEM prints last.
ferx keeps a running log-sum-exp of the joint density per subject over its convergence phase
(one draw per iteration, scored under the parameters the iteration ends with; with the step
$\gamma_k = 1/(k-K_1)$ the stochastic-approximation average is this plain mean), so the
objective costs nothing beyond the NLL cache the E-step already refreshes.

This was established on NONMEM 7.6.0 with a linear-Gaussian model where the posterior
expectation $E[-2\log p]$ and the marginal are closed-form, and it explains the offset the
committed SAEM runs show against the posterior expectation: the log of a mean of many posterior
draws sits $n_\eta(\ln 2 - 1) = -0.307$ per subject per random effect below $E[-2\log p]$
(`linear_gaussian_offset_from_the_posterior_expectation_is_ln2_minus_one` reproduces it in closed
form). On the ten committed runs `(SAEMOBJ − E[−2 log p]) / (N·n_η)` is 0.299–0.323, mean 0.312
(a non-Gaussian posterior moves it; a constant `1 − ln 2 = 0.307`, `ln(2π)/6 = 0.306` or
`1/π = 0.318` each sits within 2.5 standard errors of that mean but none within the scatter, which
is why the closed-form experiment, not the anchors, settles it). `IMP EONLY=1` prints the marginal
`−2 log L` without `N_obs·log 2π` and with the `NIND·NETA·log 2π` term, which is what ferx's
importance-sampled readout reports.

A complete ferx SAEM fit (default settings, the committed `*_fit.ferx` models) against NONMEM's
own printed SAEMOBJ. Both sides are one Monte-Carlo run with its own estimates, so the
difference is the two runs' spread, not a convention gap:

| anchor | NONMEM `SAEMOBJ` | ferx | (ferx − NONMEM) / (N·n_η) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `covmuref_additive_saem` | −1855.592 | −1856.433 | −0.007 |
| `covmuref_power_saem` | −1887.202 | −1887.145 | +0.000 |
| `covmuref_shared_saem` | −2210.147 | −2208.459 | +0.011 |
| `covmuref_anchor_a_saem` | −2210.552 | −2216.564 | −0.040 |
| `covmuref_anchor_b_saem` | −2210.896 | −2216.564 | −0.038 |
| `logit_fraction_saem` (ODE) | −4603.996 | −4604.612 | −0.003 |
| `saem_additive_mu` | 151.755 | 151.604 | −0.025 |

The worst is 0.040 per subject per random effect, a fifth of the 0.31 by which the posterior
expectation differs, and `src/estimation/saem_objective_tests.rs` asserts 0.04 on the three
fastest anchors.

#### Where it is reported, and explicit stages {#saem-ofv-where}


- **Console / summary file:** the OFV row reads `OFV (SAEM objective, NONMEM SAEMOBJ convention; not a likelihood)`
  (or `OFV (IS -2LL, NONMEM IMP EONLY=1; MC SE = …, K = …)`, `OFV (AGQ -2LL, n nodes)`), followed by `FOCE/Laplace OFV (diagnostic)`. The verbose progress
  line `SAEM completed. FOCE/Laplace OFV = …` is that diagnostic, printed before the covariance step.
- **`fit.yaml`:** `objective_function` carries `ofv_type: saem_objective` (or `importance_sampling`, `agq`),
  `ofv_mc_standard_error`, `ofv_n_samples` (or `ofv_n_nodes`) and `ofv_foce_laplace`. A
  `saem_ofv = focei` fit carries none of these.
- **R / Rust:** `FitResult.saem_objective` (`fit$saem_objective`) holds the kind, SE, sample or
  node count and `foce_ofv`; `FitResult.importance_sampling` holds the full IS result (ESS,
  low-ESS subjects). Both are stored in `.fitrx`.

To compare a SAEM fit with a FOCE/FOCEI fit, use `saem_objective.foce_ofv` (or set
`saem_ofv = focei`); the two numbers are different integrals and are not interchangeable.

**Explicit stages still work.** `method = [saem, imp]` with `imp_eval_only = true` is the same
workflow spelled out: its IS value (at `imp_samples`, default 1000) becomes the reported `ofv`
under the default and under `saem_ofv = imp`, with `saem_ofv_samples` unused. A chain with its own evaluator stage
(`imp_eval_only`, or `agq_eval_only` with a trailing `laplace`) is never given a second readout.
`imp_eval_only = true` is required for the `imp` stage: without it the stage is an estimator
(NONMEM `METHOD=IMP`) and re-fits θ/Ω/σ.

The IS evaluation starts each subject's proposal from the final EBE refinement in
step 1 and adapts it over `imp_adapt_passes` pilot passes (default 5; see
[Adaptive evaluation](importance-sampling.qmd#adaptive-evaluation)), so for a
subject still listed under `low_ess_subjects`, check that refinement's EBE and
Hessian first. See
[Importance Sampling (IMP)](importance-sampling.qmd#evaluation-only-mode-imp_eval_only-true).

#### Cost and node count {#saem-ofv-cost}

The readout runs once, after the iterations: `imp_adapt_passes` pilot passes that fit each
subject's proposal (default 5) and one final pass of `saem_ofv_samples` draws. The pilots
draw `saem_ofv_pilot_samples` each (default 300, a tenth of K), so the readout costs
`5 × 300 + 3000` posterior evaluations per subject rather than the `6 × 3000` of full-size
pilots. The final pass is always K, so the estimate stays unbiased; the pilots only place the
proposal. Measured on `pk1_saem` (500 subjects, 3 random effects): MC SE 0.454 at full-size
pilots, 0.467 at 500, 0.475 at 300 (the default), 0.487 at 200; the minimum per-subject
ESS/K goes 0.72, 0.69, 0.66, 0.61, and the value moves by 0.02–0.13, well inside the SE.
`saem_ofv_pilot_samples = 0` restores full-size pilots, which is bit-identical to the readout
before the option existed.

Measured as user-space instructions (`--threads 1`, 500 subjects × 6 observations, 3 random
effects; the `focei` column is the pre-#2973 behaviour, identical code up to the readout):

| bench fit | `focei` | `imp`, full-size pilots | `imp` (default) | `agq` (11 nodes) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `pk1_saem` (analytic, 150 + 250) | 27.47 G | 96.43 G (3.5×) | 44.23 G (1.6×) | ≈ 1.13× |
| `pk1_saem_short` (analytic, short schedule) | 3.49 G | 72.45 G (21×) | 20.25 G (5.8×) | ≈ 2.0× |
| `pk1_ode_saem` (ODE, 150 + 250) | 81.58 G | 365.72 G (4.5×) | 152.16 G (1.9×) | ≈ 1.09× |

What remains is the likelihood itself: 30% of the readout is `exp`/`expm1`/`log` in the
closed-form prediction, the individual-parameter program and the Student-t density, and the
draws are the same draws a NONMEM `EONLY=1` iteration makes. The readout is a fixed cost per
subject, so it dominates a short schedule and is a minority of a full one. Lower
`saem_ofv_samples` (the standard error scales as 1/√K), or choose `saem_ofv = agq` on a
model with up to three random effects, where it costs a twentieth as much;
`saem_ofv = focei` skips it. The estimates and sdtab are bit-identical under all of them,
since the readout never feeds back into the fit.

The node count default is measured. On `pk1_saem` the `agq` readout gives 5224.76, 5221.22, 5220.31 and 5220.21
at 5, 7, 11 and 15 nodes, against 5220.28 ± 0.18 and 5220.41 ± 0.18 from the importance
sampler at K = 20000 (two seeds), and 5219.9, 5219.8, 5219.5 (± 0.45) at the default
K = 3000 (three seeds). Eleven nodes is 0.1 from the 15-node value, where seven is 1.0
away, so 11 is the default. The two evaluators agree where both are converged.


#### NONMEM validation {#saem-ofv-nonmem}

The importance sampler is checked against NONMEM `METHOD=SAEM` followed by
`METHOD=IMP EONLY=1 NITER=10 ISAMPLE=3000` on the committed SAEM anchors
(`nonmem_anchor/results/*.ext`, NONMEM 7.5.1). ferx evaluates its sampler at
**NONMEM's own SAEM estimates** (`THETA`, `OMEGA`, `SIGMA` from the SAEM table), so both
numbers are the same integral at the same point and must agree within their Monte-Carlo
errors. NONMEM's error is the spread of its ten evaluation iterations (each an independent
K = 3000 draw); ferx's is `mc_standard_error`. The SAEM table's own objective (`SAEMOBJ`)
is shown to make the point of the change: it is not a likelihood, and it sits 700–1000
units from the exact marginal.

| anchor | NONMEM `SAEMOBJ` | NONMEM `EONLY` (SE) | ferx IS at NONMEM's estimates (SE) | diff | z |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `covmuref_shared_saem` (#1620) | −2210.147 | −1199.382 (0.300) | −1199.331 (0.155) | +0.050 | +0.15 |
| `covmuref_additive_saem` (#619) | −1855.592 | −1178.442 (0.202) | −1178.691 (0.128) | −0.249 | −1.04 |

(`tests/mixture_nonmem.rs`: ferx IS against NONMEM 300.8707) and the FREM reprex
(`frem.qmd`: ferx 6866.6 ± 1.2 against NONMEM 7.6 6869.7, sd 1.2, at the same estimates).
NONMEM's `METHOD=SAEM` run is one chain's draw, so ferx's own SAEM estimates differ a little
from NONMEM's; that difference, not the objective, is what separates the two engines'
reported values on a default fit.

### Covariance step on a non-Gaussian model {#saem-covariance-non-gaussian}

SAEM, IMP and IMPMAP estimate the *exact* marginal likelihood. The covariance step
differentiates a deterministic objective at their estimate, and by default that objective is
FOCEI's, a Laplace approximation. On an all-Gaussian model the two minima are close, which is
what the NONMEM anchors of these methods pin. With a TTE, `[binary_model]` or CTMM endpoint
they need not be: on `examples/tte_exponential.ferx` the exact minimum is at ω² = 0.071 and
the FOCEI minimum at ω² = 0.29, so at the samplers' estimates the FOCEI R matrix was
indefinite, and the eigenvalue floor turned it into standard errors of 4–10 under
`covariance_method = r` and 1e4–4e4 under `rsr` (#1781).

For `saem`, `imp` and `impmap` on such a model, R and S are now taken on the **7-node
adaptive Gauss–Hermite marginal** — the objective of `method = laplace, n_agq = 7`, which is
the exact marginal to quadrature accuracy — and the fit carries a `W_COV_QUADRATURE_OBJECTIVE`
note saying so. Seven nodes per random effect: on the example above the ω² standard error
moves by 2e-4 relative between seven and nine nodes, and is 11% low at three. The grid is
`7^n_eta` nodes per subject, so the route takes up to three random effects. A mixture, a model
with inter-occasion variability, or more than three random effects keeps the FOCEI objective
and carries `W_COV_QUADRATURE_DECLINED`, whose remedy is to polish the estimate with a FOCEI
stage.

| `tte_exponential`, SE(λ) | `r` before | `r` after | `rsr` before | `rsr` after | `s` before | `s` after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SAEM (λ = 0.03876) | 4.24 | 0.00859 | 1.3e4 | 0.00863 | 0.00854 | 0.00856 |
| IMP (λ = 0.03385) | 8.82 | 0.00818 | 3.6e4 | 0.00821 | 0.00830 | 0.00817 |
| IMPMAP (λ = 0.03359) | 9.76 | 0.00819 | 4.1e4 | 0.00823 | 0.00829 | 0.00815 |
| exact marginal, at its minimum | | 0.00818 | | 0.00823 | | 0.00813 |
| NONMEM IMP (λ = 0.03370) | | 0.00840 | | 0.00835 | | 0.00847 |

The exact-marginal row is computed outside ferx (brute-force quadrature over η); it is what
`tests/sampler_covariance_non_gaussian.rs` bands each estimator against. `s` moves too,
because its per-subject scores are now the quadrature marginal's rather than FOCEI's. Taken at
each sampler's *own* estimate instead, the same oracle agrees with every routed `r`, `s` and
`rsr` SE to about 2e-3 relative — the default `fd_hessian_step` sets that, not the node
count. SAEM's
row is the furthest off because its estimate is: its exact −2 log L is 166.879 against 166.527
at the minimum, where IMP and IMPMAP are within 0.001.

Separately, wherever R needs an eigenvalue floor (it is indefinite, or has an eigenvalue
under `max(1e-10·λ_max, 1e-12)`) at an estimate its objective was never
minimised at — a SAEM, IMP, IMPMAP or VI estimate — `r` and `rsr` no longer invert the
floored matrix (`rsr` squared the floor): the step returns `S⁻¹` instead and says so in
`W_COV_NON_STATIONARY_ESTIMATE`, or fails with that code when S is singular too. On
`examples/ctmm_pd_2state.ferx`, whose clearance and volume are not separately identified,
that is what happens after SAEM: no method gives that model usable standard errors, and the
step now says why instead of reporting SEs of 1e2–5e7.
The same fallback applies to an all-Gaussian SAEM, IMP or VI fit whose R needs the floor.
There it is tested for which matrix it returns and how it is labelled, not yet against an
external reference.

### Is the estimate a stationary point? {#saem-stationarity}

Whether R needs the floor does not say whether the estimate is stationary: R can be positive
definite well away from the objective's minimum. So after a SAEM, IMP, IMPMAP or VI fit
whose R was kept, the step also takes the gradient g of the objective R differentiates, at the
estimate, and its Newton decrement ½·gᵀH⁻¹g, H the OFV Hessian
([#2541](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2541)). That is the OFV a Newton step
would remove, and also the squared distance from the estimate to the objective's minimum,
measured in the standard errors of R⁻¹ (under `covariance_method = rsr` the reported
standard errors are the sandwich's, and the message says so). Above 1 OFV unit (one standard error) the step adds
`W_COV_NON_STATIONARY_ESTIMATE`, giving the decrement and how to get SEs at a stationary
point. It still returns the R-based standard errors: S⁻¹ is no better at that point, since
its per-subject scores carry the non-zero mean gradient. The cost is one gradient evaluation,
exact where the analytic outer gradient is and otherwise `2·n_free` objective evaluations.
`report_final_gradient = false` does not skip it: that option turns off a reported number,
and skipping this gradient would drop the warning instead.

The threshold was measured on Linux, the reference platform for fit numbers:

| model | fit | decrement (OFV units) | warns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `warfarin`, `two_cpt_oral_cov`, `mbma_placebo`, `warfarin_iov_saem`, `tte_exponential` | FOCE / FOCEI | ≤ 7e-9 | no |
| `warfarin`, `two_cpt_oral_cov` | SAEM (4 seeds), IMP, IMPMAP | 8e-6 – 0.082 | no |
| `tte_exponential` (7-node quadrature objective) | SAEM (2 seeds), IMP, IMPMAP | 3e-4 – 0.343 | no |
| `warfarin_iov_saem` | SAEM, `seed = 2` (0.43 OFV above FOCEI) | 0.415 | no |
| `two_cpt_oral_cov`, full 5×5 `block_omega` (23 free parameters) | SAEM 500 + 2000 iterations, IMPMAP (0.09 OFV above FOCEI) | 0.087 / 0.094 | no |
| the same block model | SAEM, `seed = 3` (22.7 OFV above FOCEI) | 1.05 | yes |
| `warfarin`, `two_cpt_oral_cov`, the block model | VI (1.3–3.2 OFV above FOCEI) | 1.43 / 3.24 / 3.44 | yes |
| `tests/data/mbma_placebo` | SAEM, 5 runs with positive-definite R (1.3–3.6 OFV above FOCEI) | 1.46 – 5.35 | yes |

macOS gives the same numbers on every model except `mbma_placebo`, where SAEM takes a
different path and stops further from the optimum (decrements 4.0–14.9).

On `mbma_placebo` this is what flags the `seed = 2` fit
([below](#saem-standard-errors)).

The test is local. An estimate at or near a *different* stationary point passes it: SAEM
with `seed = 2` on `two_cpt_oral_cov` stops 39 OFV above the FOCEI minimum with a decrement
of 0.25, and `seed = 12345` on the block model 29 OFV above with 0.41.

### Standard errors at a SAEM estimate {#saem-standard-errors}

The covariance step reads R and S off the FOCEI objective (or the quadrature marginal above)
at SAEM's estimate. SAEM approximates its minimum stochastically, so on a weakly identified
model the estimate can stop away from it even when both objectives share their minimum. On
the 6-study `tests/data/mbma_placebo` model, η enters linearly with a fixed residual, so FOCEI
*is* the exact likelihood (minimum −2 log L 97.07). Five SAEM runs (three seeds at the
default length, two at 500 + 2000 iterations) stopped 1–11 units above that, all reporting
`converged` ([#2536](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2536); macOS arm64; on Linux
the same runs stop 1.3–11.6 units above, seed 2 at 98.35 with a decrement of 1.46, which warns
too). The cause was
that model's one-line `BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_E0 + KAPPA_ARM`, which before
[#2544](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2544) left TVE0 un-mu-referenced.
With TVE0 mu-referenced, SAEM on seeds 12345, 2, 3, 7, 11 lands at 97.33–98.39 for
`E0 = TVE0 + ETA_E0` on a line of its own and, since #2544, at 97.21–98.88 for the
one-line spelling (macOS arm64; per seed the two differ, since the sums associate
differently, but the spread is the same —
[Additive mu-references](#saem-mstep-additive)). The rows below are the one-line model
before #2544, the shape a line whose theta is also read elsewhere still has:

| fit | −2 log L | TVE0 | ω² | covariance step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FOCEI | 97.07 | 48.58 ± 0.95 | 4.81 ± 2.99 | computed |
| SAEM, default seed | 107.92 | 43.85 | 30.3 | fails, `W_COV_NON_STATIONARY_ESTIMATE` |
| SAEM, `seed = 2` | 102.10 | 46.65 ± 2.82 | 10.7 ± 14.8 | computed, `W_COV_NON_STATIONARY_ESTIMATE` (decrement 14.9) |

Whether R is positive definite at such a point decides only which form of
`W_COV_NON_STATIONARY_ESTIMATE` the step gives, not whether the estimate is stationary: the
two SAEM rows are equally far from it. The default seed fails; at `seed = 2` the SEs are
reported, with the gradient form of the warning ([above](#saem-stationarity); before
[#2541](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/ferx-core/issues/2541) they came with none). They are 3×
(TVE0) and 5× (ω²) the FOCEI ones; do not report them as SEs of the fit. What
works:

- **`method = [saem, focei]`.** The FOCEI stage finishes at the FOCEI minimum and takes R
  there. Its estimates and SEs are FOCEI's (on the model above, equal to a plain FOCEI fit to
  six figures), not the SAEM estimate's. For an all-Gaussian model this is the fit to report
  SEs from.
- **`sir = true`** samples a proposal built from R with its eigenvalues made positive,
  weighted by the FOCEI objective (FOCE without interaction), whose minimum need not be the
  SAEM estimate. On the model above it ran with an effective sample size of 21 of
  1000, and its TVE0 interval [45.1, 51.2] excludes the SAEM estimate, because the weights pull
  towards the FOCEI minimum.
- **`covariance_method = s`** needs more subjects than free parameters: S is a sum of one
  rank-one term per subject. With 6 subjects and 24 free parameters it is singular at every
  estimate, which the failure message states. `rsr` never inverts S but needs R positive
  definite.

## Conditional Distribution (conditional mode vs. distribution)

The post-SAEM finalization above produces the conditional **mode** of each
subject's random effects — the empirical Bayes estimate (EBE), the single most
probable \\( \eta_i \\). That is a point estimate. SAEM's MCMC E-step is, however,
already sampling each subject's full **conditional distribution**
\\( p(\eta_i \mid y_i; \hat\theta) \\); the mode discards everything but its peak.

Set `conddist = true` to run an opt-in post-fit pass that characterises that
distribution. With the population parameters fixed at their converged values, the
same MH kernels (block, componentwise, and the per-occasion kappa kernel for IOV)
are re-run per subject — warm-started at the EBE mode — and the draws are
*accumulated* rather than discarded. The pass reports, per subject:

- the **conditional mean** \\( \mathbb{E}[\eta_i \mid y_i] \\),
- the **conditional SD** \\( \mathrm{sd}(\eta_i \mid y_i) \\),
- optionally the raw draws (`conddist_keep_samples = true`), and
- a distribution-based **η-shrinkage**, \\( 1 - \mathrm{sd}_i(\bar\eta_i)/\omega \\),
  reported alongside the usual mode-based `shrinkage_eta`.

This mirrors the conditional-mode vs. conditional-distribution distinction in
**saemix** (`map.saemix` vs `conddist.saemix`; Comets, Lavenu & Lavielle, *J. Stat.
Soft.* 80(3), 2017) and **Monolix** (the "Conditional Mode" vs "Conditional
Distribution" tasks). Why prefer the distribution for diagnostics: EBEs and
conditional means are shrunk toward the population, so η–covariate and η–η
relationships built on them can be hidden or fabricated; samples from the
conditional distribution are not shrinkage-biased.

Results are exposed on `FitResult.cond_dist` and written by the CLI to
`{model}-conddist.csv` (`ID, ETA, COND_MEAN, COND_SD, COND_MODE`), with the raw
draws in `{model}-conddist-samples.csv` when retained.

On the bundled warfarin data (10 subjects, 1-cpt oral, log-normal CL/V/KA,

| conditional mean | 1.0000 | 0.0029 | 0.0011 |
| conditional SD   | 0.9913 | 0.0024 | 0.0009 |
| mode / MAP       | 1.0000 | 0.0002 | 0.0001 |

## Inter-Occasion Variability (IOV)

`method = saem` supports models with `kappa` declarations (`n_kappa > 0`). IOV is handled with a per-occasion Gibbs Metropolis-Hastings step interleaved with the standard eta MH:

- **E-step**: After sampling $\eta$, one MH proposal is made for each occasion's $\kappa_k$. Both the eta and kappa samplers target the correct conditional distributions: $p(\eta | \kappa, \theta, \text{data})$ and $p(\kappa_k | \eta, \theta, \text{data})$ respectively.
- **SA update**: $S_2^{\text{iov}} \leftarrow (1 - \gamma_k) S_2^{\text{iov}} + \gamma_k \cdot \frac{1}{N_{\text{occ}}} \sum_i \sum_k \kappa_{ik} \kappa_{ik}^T$
- **M-step**: $\Omega_{\text{iov}} = S_2^{\text{iov}}$ (analytic update, same structure as the BSV omega M-step).

No additional configuration is required; `method = saem` works for both BSV-only and IOV models.

## Models with no random effects are rejected

SAEM is an EM algorithm *over the random effects*. A model that declares none
(`n_eta = 0` — see [no omega at all](../model-file/parameters.qmd#no-omega-at-all-fixed-effects-only-naive-pooled-fits))
has an empty E-step: there is nothing to sample and the stochastic approximation
has nothing to average, leaving an M-step that is plain maximum likelihood on
θ/σ. Left to run, it terminates on its own criterion slightly short of the
optimum — on the `one_cpt_iv` zero-Ω anchor it reports converged at OFV −269.599
where FOCEI reaches −269.637.

Rather than return a quietly-wrong answer, `method = saem` errors at `n_eta = 0`:

```text
method = saem requires at least one random effect (n_eta = 0). SAEM is an EM over
the random effects, so with none declared its E-step is empty and it only
approaches the objective that FOCE/FOCEI minimise exactly. Use method = foce,
focei, or laplace for a fixed-effects-only (naive-pooled) model.
```

The check runs in the same validation pass as `ferx check`, and fires if `saem`
appears **anywhere** in a `method = [...]` chain — so `method = [saem, focei]`
fails up front rather than after the SAEM stage has already run.

`imp`, `impmap` and `bayes` are rejected at `n_eta = 0` in the same pass, under the
code `E_METHOD_NO_RANDOM_EFFECTS` (#1007) — each integrates over the random
effects, and with none declared the marginal likelihood collapses to the
observation likelihood FOCE/FOCEI already minimise exactly. Like the SAEM guard
this fires anywhere in a chain, so `method = [focei, imp]` fails up front instead
of after the FOCEI stage has run. Each of the three still refuses at run time as
well, which is what a direct `fit()` caller bypassing `ferx check` sees.

## Configuration

```
[fit_options]
  method        = saem
  # n_exploration = 150    # Phase 1 length; omit for the automatic stop (150..4000)
  n_exploration_min = 150  # automatic stop only
  n_exploration_max = 4000 # automatic stop only
  smoothing_exponent = 1.0 # Phase 2 step 1/(k-K1)^a
  n_convergence = 1000     # Phase 2 iterations
  n_chains      = 2        # eta chains per subject (NONMEM ISAMPLE)
  n_mh_steps    = auto     # block-MH steps/subject/iteration, or `auto` (see above)
  n_leapfrog    = 0        # Set > 0 (e.g. 3) to use HMC instead of MH
  adapt_interval = 50      # Step-size adaptation frequency (interval rule)
  scale_adaptation = interval  # or robbins_monro
  omega_burnin  = 20       # Iterations to hold Ω fixed while the chain warms up
  seed          = 12345    # RNG seed for reproducibility
  covariance    = true     # Compute standard errors

  # Conditional-distribution pass (opt-in; off by default)
  conddist              = true    # Estimate p(η_i | y_i) per subject after the fit
  conddist_nsamp        = 2000    # Retained MCMC draws per subject
  conddist_burnin       = 500     # Burn-in draws discarded before accumulation
  conddist_keep_samples = false   # Retain the raw draws (writes -conddist-samples.csv)
```

## Tuning Guide

### Not Converging

- If the fit warns that exploration reached its maximum, raise `n_exploration_max` (e.g., 4000, NONMEM's `AUTO` value); to force a length instead, set `n_exploration` (e.g., 500)
- Increase `n_convergence` (e.g., 500) for a longer averaging window
- Raise `n_mh_steps` above what `auto` resolves to (e.g. 30-50) for better
  mixing in the E-step on hard surfaces. The rule caps at 20, the count
  calibrated to escape the basin trap observed on Emax PKPD with stressful
  initial values (see below), and it reaches that cap only at 8 observations
  per subject per η; an ODE-with-Form-C readout may need more proposals than
  either to fully decorrelate samples between M-step calls.

### PD-curve thetas collapse on cold start (Emax / sigmoid readouts)

A failure mode specific to models that read population thetas through a Form
C `[scaling]` block (e.g. `y[CMT=N] = E0 + EMAX * effect^GAMMA / ...`) and
score them via a per-CMT additive `[error_model]`: from stressful initial
values (e.g. 1.5× truth) the M-step can lock the PD-curve thetas into a
degenerate basin where `E0 → 0`, `EMAX` and `EC50` blow up, and `GAMMA`
collapses below 1. The likelihood at the bad basin is only modestly worse
than at truth (~150 OFV units on a 100-subject benchmark), so SAEM doesn't
back out on its own.

The underlying cause is MCMC sample correlation: with an early default
`n_mh_steps = 3` the chain didn't decorrelate enough between SAEM outer
iterations, so the single-draw stochastic M-step received sticky correlated
ETAs that biased the population-θ update toward the basin. The default was
raised to 10 and then to 20 (alongside the componentwise kernel and the
damped Ω step), which resolves this reliably across seeds at modest extra
wall on the affected model and ~0% on simpler PK-only models.

This benchmark has 16 observations per subject against 2 η, so the `auto`
rule resolves it to the same 20: **the count that closed this trap is
unchanged on the model it was calibrated on** (#1459). Re-measuring it on
`e7343462` at 6 seeds, the boundary collapse itself no longer reproduces at
any count from 2 to 20 — `E0` lands at 1.83–2.02 against a truth of 2 and
`GAMMA` at 0.89–1.08, never at a bound — but what 20 still buys is
reproducibility along the EMAX/EC50 ridge: final-estimate distance 0.029 and
cross-seed stability 0.044 at 20, against 0.076–0.173 and 0.090–0.160 at 4–8.
That ridge is a property of the data, not of the sampler (FOCEI on the same
dataset lands at EMAX 20.0 / EC50 1.78 where SAEM lands at 53.1 / 7.28), so
report both endpoints and check several seeds on any Emax/Hill fit.

If you still see this signature (E0 hitting its lower bound, EMAX large,
EC50 large) on a related Emax/Hill model:

1. Try `n_mh_steps = 50` (above the `auto` cap of 20)
2. Warm-start from a FOCEI fit (`method = [focei, saem]`)
3. Run with several seeds and keep the lowest OFV

### Ω Collapses / Residual Error Inflates

On sparse data (few observations per subject) the variance components can collapse toward zero on the first iterations while the residual error absorbs the between-subject variability (e.g. tiny `omega` with a large additive `sigma`). The default `omega_burnin = 20` and the damped Ω SA step guard against this by keeping Ω near its starting value while the chain warms up. If it still occurs, raise `omega_burnin` (e.g. 40) and/or `n_mh_steps` so the chain reaches a representative spread before Ω is first estimated, then polish with `method = [saem, focei]`.

### Block Ω correlations near ±1 (rank-1 collapse)

For a `block_omega` (correlated) random-effects block, a faulty E-step/M-step coupling can drive **every** off-diagonal correlation toward ±1 while one variance collapses toward zero — a near rank-1 Ω that FOCEI on the same data does not show. The mechanism is the block proposal (preconditioned by `chol(Ω)`) plus the single-draw Ω M-step feeding correlation back into Ω during the `γ=1` exploration phase. ferx guards this by default with two mechanisms — the **componentwise MH kernel** and the **damped Ω SA step** described above — so on a poorly-identified 2-cpt model the SAEM Ω now matches the FOCEI/NONMEM estimate (e.g. corr(CL,V1) ≈ 0.67, corr(V1,V2) ≈ 0.4) across seeds instead of collapsing to ≈0.99. If you still see inflated block correlations, raise `n_mh_steps` (this also raises the componentwise sweep count `n_mh_steps / n_eta`) and run several seeds.

### The additive term of a `combined()` error model

Before ferx #1445 the additive component of `combined(PROP, ADD)` could be
driven onto its optimizer lower bound on sparse data where NONMEM's own SAEM
estimates a clearly non-zero value, and it got *worse* with more iterations. The
cause was the σ half of the numerical M-step being assigned outright rather than
averaged: the additive term of a combined model is often a **minority** variance
component, identified only where $\sigma_{\text{add}}$ and
$\sigma_{\text{prop}}\cdot f$ are comparable, and the conditional maximiser of a
weakly identified variance component from a single η draw sits near zero a large
fraction of the time. The [damped σ step](#stochastic-approximation-update) makes
the estimate the average of that sequence rather than its last draw.

Anchored against NONMEM 7.5.1 `METHOD=SAEM` on the same 300-subject,
median-one-observation dataset (`nonmem_anchor/saem_sparse_combined_saem.ctl`
and `data/saem_sparse_combined.csv`, which is the fixture
`tests/saem_combined_error.rs` scores; results in
`nonmem_anchor/results/saem_sparse_combined_saem.ext`, read from the `.ext`
because a SAEM+IMP chain truncates its `.lst`):

| | additive SD (truth 1.8) | proportional SD (truth 0.13) |
|---|---|---|
| NONMEM SAEM, `ISAMPLE=10` | 1.5425 | 0.1370 |
| NONMEM SAEM, `ISAMPLE=2` (its default) | 1.6463 | 0.1491 |
| ferx SAEM **after** #1445, 8 seeds | 1.42 [1.11, 1.75] | 0.139 |
| ferx SAEM **before** #1445, 3 seeds | 0.011 / 0.0025 / 0.011 | 0.135 |
| ferx FOCEI | 3.220 | 0.1200 |

ferx SAEM now agrees with NONMEM SAEM on the additive term to 8% of the
simulation truth and on the proportional term to 1.5%, where before it sat four
orders of magnitude below it. (NONMEM's `ISAMPLE=2` default collapses the two
weakly identified Ω diagonals on this design — 8.8e-4 and 0.032 against truths
0.15 and 0.69 — which is why the `ISAMPLE=10` arm is the headline; the σ
estimate moves only from 1.65 to 1.54 between them.) On a real dataset,
`ferx-testdata/cefepime_jordan` run64, NONMEM FOCEI estimates the additive RUV
at 1.550 (`nm/run64.ext`, THETA(6)); ferx SAEM reports 1.16 [0.97, 1.34] after
the change and ~1e-3 before it.

Note what the objective does **not** say here: on the simulated fixture the
importance-sampled −2 log L is 3183.1 after against 3183.4 before, a 0.2
difference that is pure noise. That is not a defect in the comparison, it is the
whole problem restated — a minority variance component is weakly identified, the
likelihood is nearly flat in it, and an estimator that reports a single draw of
a flat direction will wander to the boundary while barely moving the objective.
Rank the two by the parameter against a known truth and an external engine, not
by the likelihood they are nearly tied on.

The price is that σ now *lags*: it is a Robbins-Monro average over the
convergence phase, so a run that is too short reports a σ still on its way down
from the starting guess. If σ has clearly not settled, lengthen the run
(`n_exploration` first, so averaging starts from an equilibrated chain) rather
than reading the last value. If `ADD` still lands on its bound, it is genuinely
not identified by the data — check it (RSE, σ-correlation, profile likelihood)
rather than assuming the estimator.

### IIV on residual error (`iiv_on_ruv`): σ × ω_RUV ridge

With `iiv_on_ruv = ETA`, the residual is $Y = f + \varepsilon \exp(\eta_{\text{RUV}})$, so the residual variance is $\sigma^2 \exp(2\eta_{\text{RUV}})$. This form is invariant to $\eta_{\text{RUV}} \to \eta_{\text{RUV}} - c,\ \sigma \to \sigma\,e^{c}$ — $\sigma$ and a *shift* of $\eta_{\text{RUV}}$ are a degenerate pair. Unlike a mu-referenced structural $\eta$ (whose mean is folded into its typical value $\theta$ each M-step), $\eta_{\text{RUV}}$ has **no typical-value $\theta$**, so nothing absorbs its mean: it drifts along that degenerate direction, and because $\omega_{\text{RUV}}$ is estimated as $\overline{\eta_{\text{RUV}}^2}$ the drift injects a spurious $\text{mean}^2$ term that pumps $\sigma$ and $\omega_{\text{RUV}}$ **up together** — the runaway reported in issue #895 ($\omega_{\text{RUV}}$ toward ~49, $\sigma$ toward its e⁵ ceiling), worst on FREM models with an extreme $\Omega$-diagonal scale range.

ferx fixes this by treating $\sigma$ as the residual-scale typical value: each iteration $\eta_{\text{RUV}}$ is **re-centred to zero mean**, absorbing the shift into $\sigma$ ($\eta_{\text{RUV}} \mathrel{-}= \overline{\eta_{\text{RUV}}}$, every RUV-scaled $\sigma \mathrel{\times}= e^{\overline{\eta_{\text{RUV}}}}$). Each subject's residual variance is exactly unchanged, so the likelihood is untouched, but $E[\eta_{\text{RUV}}]=0$ is restored and $\omega_{\text{RUV}}$ measures the true variance. On the 475-subject FREM reprex this converges from both a too-small and a too-large $\sigma$ start, where it previously ran to $\omega_{\text{RUV}} \approx 49$. Re-measured on 2026-10-16 from the 5.5×-low start, it reaches $\omega_{\text{RUV}} = 0.269$, $\sigma = 0.174$ and an importance-sampled −2 log L of 6866.6 ± 1.2. NONMEM IMP reports 0.279 / 0.177 / 6852 ([FREM: `iiv_on_ruv`](frem.qmd#frem-iiv-on-ruv), which also covers why FOCEI is not an alternative on that model). Re-centring is applied only when **every** RUV-scaled $\sigma$ component is free to absorb the shift — this keeps each subject's residual variance exactly unchanged. If any residual $\sigma$ component is FIXed (e.g. a fixed additive term of a combined error), scaling only the free component would leave the fixed part uncompensated, so re-centring is skipped and the growth caps below carry the load (a FIXed $\sigma$ already partially pins the mean).

Two growth caps remain as belt-and-braces backstops, both no-ops on a well-behaved fit:

- **σ growth cap** — each free RUV-scaled residual $\sigma$ is capped at $\approx 20\times$ its scale (a post-M-step clamp). A $\sigma$ whose own user upper bound is already tighter carries no separate cap — NLopt enforces that bound directly.
- **ω_RUV growth cap** — the RUV $\Omega$ variance is capped at $\approx 20\times$ its scale, applied as a correlation-preserving rescale of the RUV row/column so a block $\Omega$ stays positive-definite. A FIXed off-diagonal covariance with the RUV eta is left exactly as declared.

The reference "scale" is the *larger* of the starting value and the data-informed value the fit reaches by the end of the exploration phase, so a run started from a $\sigma$/$\omega_{\text{RUV}}$ guess many-fold below the truth is not spuriously clamped. If either cap ever binds (it should not, now that the drift is removed), SAEM warns that the split is weakly identified and suggests fixing $\sigma$.

### Slow Convergence

- Decrease `n_exploration` and `n_convergence` if parameters stabilize early
- Use `adapt_interval = 25` for faster step-size adaptation, or
  `scale_adaptation = robbins_monro` when the acceptance-rate warning says the
  scales never reached their target

### Reproducibility

- Always set `seed` for reproducible results
- Different seeds will produce slightly different estimates due to the stochastic nature of the algorithm

## Output

The SAEM iteration progress is printed to stderr:

```
SAEM: 10 subjects, 3 ETAs, 400 total iter (150 explore + 250 converge)
  SAEM iter    1/400 [explore] γ=1.000  condNLL=95.244
  SAEM iter   50/400 [explore] γ=1.000  condNLL=56.705
  SAEM iter  150/400 [explore] γ=1.000  condNLL=46.071
  SAEM iter  200/400 [converge] γ=0.020  condNLL=36.799
  SAEM iter  400/400 [converge] γ=0.004  condNLL=38.096
SAEM iterations complete. Computing final EBEs and OFV...
SAEM completed. FOCE/Laplace OFV = ...
Running covariance step...
```

The `FOCE/Laplace OFV = ...` line is printed **before** the covariance step starts (#893). It is the diagnostic value; the reported OFV (NONMEM's SAEM objective by default, the importance-sampled `−2 log L` under `saem_ofv = imp`) follows in the final report. See [The reported OFV](#saem-reported-ofv).
SAEM only learns its OFV at the very end (the final FOCE approximation), and the
covariance matrix is often the most expensive part of the run — so seeing the OFV
first lets you interrupt (Ctrl-C) when the OFV already rules the run out, instead of
waiting for a covariance matrix you won't use.

### Why `γ` (gamma) is shown

$\gamma_k$ is the **stochastic-approximation step size**, not a model quantity — it is intrinsic to the SAEM algorithm and tells you which phase the run is in and how aggressively the estimates are still moving:

- **Exploration** (`[explore]`, $k \le K_1$): $\gamma_k = 1$. Each iteration fully replaces the running sufficient statistics, so the chain roams freely toward the basin of the MLE.
- **Convergence** (`[converge]`, $k > K_1$): $\gamma_k = 1/(k - K_1)$ decays toward zero. Updates shrink into a decreasing-weight average that damps the Monte-Carlo noise so the estimates settle. The printed value (e.g. `0.020`, `0.004`) is exactly this decaying weight applied to the Ω, θ, and σ updates each iteration.

### Why `condNLL` and not `OFV`

During the iterations ferx prints `condNLL`, the **conditional** (joint) negative log-likelihood summed over subjects, evaluated at the *current MH/HMC-sampled* etas:

$$
\text{condNLL} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \text{NLL}(\eta_i^{\text{sampled}})
$$

This is a cheap per-iteration progress signal. It is **not** the marginal objective function value (OFV): it is evaluated at one stochastic draw of the random effects rather than integrated over their distribution, so unlike the FOCE/FOCEI outer-loop OFV it is noisy, will not decrease monotonically, and is **not comparable across runs** for model selection.

The reported **OFV** is computed only once, after the iterations finish: by default NONMEM's SAEM objective (one refinement of the conditional modes), or under `saem_ofv = imp` the marginal $-2 \log L$ importance-sampled as NONMEM's `IMP EONLY=1`, which is expensive; the `FOCE/Laplace OFV = ...` line is the Laplace diagnostic computed first. See [Post-SAEM Finalization](#post-saem-finalization).

(`NLL` = *negative log-likelihood*, i.e. $-\log L$. NONMEM's `OFV = -2 \log L` is essentially `2 × NLL` plus a constant.)

`condNLL` should generally decrease during the exploration phase and stabilize during convergence.
